The Spring Boot Mastery Book
Show me the mechanism. Then show me the system. From your first bean to the architect's chair, in seventeen incidents and one hostile review. Spring Boot 4 / Spring Framework 7 / Java 21.
Otmane Omry
Software Engineer & Développeur Full Stack · Java, Spring Boot, React, Angular
otmaneomry.github.io · linkedin.com/in/omryotmane

v2.4, November 10, 2026 · pure-Java edition · runnable labs in labs/ · version history in Appendix I · version-sensitive facts audited in docs/VERSION-CLAIMS.md

What this is. This book follows the roadmap.sh/spring-boot tree, with every topic weighted toward what a senior architect needs in 2026. Some things are left out on purpose: Appendix H lists the omissions and where to study them. The book is taught as one continuous story, built to carry a reader from a first Spring bean to senior-architect judgment. The protagonist, Kenza, spent eight years writing frameworkless Java at Meridian Freight, a logistics firm allergic to frameworks: object graphs hand-wired in main(), raw JDBC, an embedded Jetty configured line by line. She knows Java well and Spring not at all when she joins the team behind a bug-bounty platform. One year of outages, audits, lost updates and 3 a.m. pages rebuilds her from someone who hand-wires everything into a principal architect. Every chapter is a realistic production incident that forces one roadmap topic to senior depth. Then the chapter climbs to the system-level call behind it: which quality attribute was at stake, what the decision record says, which alternatives lost and why. You remember the concepts through what happened to Kenza, and you practice deciding what she should do next before the text tells you.
Who this book is for. This book is written for two kinds of reader. If you know core Java (generics, collections, lambdas, basic concurrency) and basic SQL but nothing about Spring, you sit in Kenza's seat. You learn every mechanism with her, from first principles. Core Java is the only hard prerequisite, but the climb is fast, and the Part primers are your handholds. Each Part opens with a half-page primer in plain prose on its core nouns. Read it if Spring is new to you, and skip it without loss if Spring is your day job. If you already run Spring in production, read the same incidents for what sits above the mechanism: styles, boundaries, consistency, the -ilities, the decision reps. Every chapter opens at a level a beginner can reach and climbs to the architecture on top, and it talks down to neither reader. The arc inside every chapter is the arc of the book: mechanic → senior → architect.
Lineage. This is the pure-Java edition. Its prose, cast, incidents, four-beat debriefs and architect layer evolved from earlier drafts that are not published here. It ships with companion artifacts. examples/ holds commented .java drill files, one folder per topic. labs/ is a multi-module Maven project (Spring Boot 4 · Java 21) with six labs: a first application you can run, then five of this book's traps as green tests you can break yourself (cd labs && ./mvnw test).


How to read this book
Four passes, each at its own speed:

The story pass: read it like a novel. The book asks one thing of you: at every ⏸ Your call beat, stop and commit to an answer, out loud or in a margin note, before you read the reveal. The plot pauses exactly where an architect would have to decide. Predicting is the rep: retrieval practice disguised as suspense.
The debrief pass: go back to the ## The debrief sections only. Each one opens with the chapter's kill-shot (the interview question the chapter prepares you to answer) and its follow-ups. Answer aloud for 90 seconds before you read on, then tick each of the four beats you said: claim, mechanism, trade-off, failure mode. Three ticks pass. With fewer, re-read the scene named in the story anchors and try again the next day. The model answer follows below a rule, in the same four beats (Claim → Mechanism → Trade-off → Failure mode). After it come THE ARCHITECT'S LENS (which -ility was at stake, what the ADR records, which alternatives were rejected and why), the story anchors and the interview ammo. Every chapter has one kill-shot, numbered by chapter: kill-shot 3 is Chapter 3's question.
The decision pass: replay only the ⚖ Your move, architect forks. Each is a realistic decision with three options. Commit, then check your reasoning against the revealed trade-offs. Most forks replay a decision you just watched. For those, argue the losing options at full strength before the reveal. Ch.15 hands you the rubric instead of the answer, and Ch.16 and 17 hand you the pen. One warning from the index in Appendix D.1: the balanced option wins often but not always. It loses outright at least twice, and one winning call is overturned at the hostile review. If you catch yourself picking the moderate option by pattern instead of analysis, you've stopped doing the rep. Watch which kind of door each decision is. Two-way decisions reward keeping options open. One-way doors (the public contract, the consistency model) reward committing decisively on today's information. At least two forks in this book are one-way doors where "keep it purchasable" is the documented trap.
The anchor drill: cover the page, recall the scene (the 28-second dashboard…), re-derive the mechanism, then name the -ility it threatened. If the scene won't surface both, re-read that chapter.

The four-week path. If you have an interview date, read, run and say aloud on this schedule; a chapter takes about 35 minutes to read and 10 to drill.

The recall hooks:

B.E.A.N.S.: Bootstrap · Endpoints · Access-to-data · Non-functional · Scale.
The Request Journey: socket → connector → filter chain → DispatcherServlet → controller → @Transactional proxy → repository → persistence context → DB → back. It is born on the Wall in Chapter 5, annotated all year, and diagrammed in Appendix E.
The senior answer skeleton: Claim → Mechanism → Trade-off → Failure mode. It is Rachid's whole curriculum, in four beats.
The -ilities ledger: scalability · availability · evolvability · performance · security · operability · cost, plus the ones that specific incidents add (integrity, maintainability, testability). They are the architect's subject: every major decision in this book names which of them it serves and which it taxes. An answer that names no -ility is a developer answer.
The ADR trail: Glasshouse numbers its Architecture Decision Records, and so does this book. When a chapter mints one (context → decision → consequences, half a page, dated), it joins the trail in Appendix F. A decision you can't show a record for gets re-litigated forever.
The story anchors: every gotcha is welded to a scene. Recall the scene, and the mechanism comes with it.

A note on temperature. The chapters run hot by design, and the incident prose stays hot. The flat ground is deliberate and lives elsewhere: the plain-prose primers before each Part and the debriefs after each chapter are the rest stops. Use them that way, because the narration will not slow down for you.
Spaced callbacks. From Chapter 2 onward, each chapter deliberately brings back one or two earlier incidents ("this is February's proxy ghost wearing a new coat"). When you hit a callback, pause one beat and re-derive the original mechanism from memory before reading on. That is the spacing schedule at work.

The cast



Who
Role
Why they matter




Kenza
Protagonist. Eight years of frameworkless Java at Meridian Freight: hand-wired object graphs, raw JDBC, Jetty configured by hand. Strong Java, zero Spring
Her plain-Java instincts are the book's recurring device: sometimes a head start, sometimes the trap. Her arc: humbled → mechanic → debugger → teacher → incident commander → system decider → architect. Watch how early she starts making calls about Atrium instead of about code.


Rachid
Principal architect, employee #4, stepping back at year's end
Reviews in green ink and answers questions with smaller questions. His catchphrase ("Show me the mechanism") is the book's thesis. His quieter second question is "and which -ility does it spend?"


Imane
Junior engineer, joins in June
The mirror arc: she asks the questions everyone avoids and ships the book's second self-invocation bug. She ends the year receiving the Chapter-1 treatment from Kenza.


Youssef
SRE / platform engineer
Owns Kubernetes, on-call, and the Monday brick ceremony. The voice of operational debt, and so of operability, the -ility developers forget until 3 a.m.


Leila
Product manager
Every technical failure reaches her as money: the cost column of the ledger. She argues the user's side of every trade-off and teaches Kenza that stating a trade-off is a negotiation, not a lecture.


@sable
Top external researcher on the platform's own program
Never appears in person, only through reports, retest comments and one late-night email. The book's conscience: the outside world, always testing your claims.

Triage lead
The human face of the workflows the code keeps breaking. Because of her, "data integrity" always has a name attached.



The company: Glasshouse is a bug-bounty and vulnerability-disclosure platform (a mini HackerOne). Companies run Programs, Researchers submit Reports, Triagers validate and route them, and Admins manage programs and payouts. The core system is a seven-year-old Spring monolith codenamed Atrium (Spring Boot 4.0.x, Java 21, Maven, PostgreSQL, Kubernetes). It is later fronted by a gateway, with one service split out where the seam is real. Glasshouse dogfoods itself through its own public program, Stonethrow, because people who live in glass houses should invite the stones.
The furniture (recurring memory anchors):

The Wall: the do-not-erase whiteboard where the Request Journey is born (Ch.5) and annotated all year. It also accumulates the context map: the borders inside Atrium that eventually decide what splits and what stays.
"Show me the mechanism.": Rachid's catchphrase. It passes down the succession chain until Imane hears it from Kenza in the book's final line.
The Canary: the dented rubber canary on the desk of whoever owns the gnarliest bug. You explain the problem to it, out loud, before you may escalate to a human.
The Brick: the pager-shaped relic handed over every Monday with whatever on-call wisdom the outgoing person has the dignity to admit.
The green pen: Rachid reviews on paper, in green. Where the pen ends up is how the book ends.
The ADR binder: a thin, unglamorous folder in the repo, docs/adr/. It starts this book nearly empty and fills as you read.


Contents
Part I: The Craft

The Review. Her first PR gets 47 green-ink comments. Clean code, SOLID, constructor injection and DTOs at the boundary, with the dependency rule, the first seam of a modular monolith, and ADR-001 underneath them.

Part II: The Container

The Container. A startup crash and a cross-user data leak. IoC/DI, scopes, the bean lifecycle and circular dependencies, then architecture as something you enforce (fitness functions).
Smoke and Mirrors. Triage updates half-save in production. AOP, proxies and self-invocation, then the boundary between leaning on the framework and fighting it.
The Magic Show. A dependency bump makes a bean vanish, only in prod. Auto-configuration, conditions and config precedence, then evolvability as a supply-chain property.

Part III: The Request

The Front Door. @sable reports that the API leaks its floor plan. The Request Journey, validation and ProblemDetail, then API design as contract governance.
The Pool. Launch-day 503s with idle CPUs. Thread-per-request, pool exhaustion and timeouts, then availability math: queues, bulkheads, blast radius.

Part IV: The Data

The Thousand Queries. The 28-second dashboard. Persistence context, N+1 and LazyInitializationException, then performance as a designed property.
The Silent Commit. Half-saved failures and lost updates. Transactions, rollback rules and locking, then consistency models chosen on purpose.
The Proxy You Didn't Write. Spring Data, projections, migrations and pool sizing, then the aggregate boundary, where DDD starts paying rent.

Part V: Production

The Breach That Wasn't. @sable's critical against Glasshouse itself. The filter chain, JWT and CSRF/CORS, then security architecture: token boundaries, trust zones, zero-trust posture.
Forty Minutes. The CI suite nobody trusts. Slices, context caching and Testcontainers, then the test pyramid as an architectural fitness function.
Three A.M. Paged blind, and later Kubernetes kills healthy pods. Actuator, probes and metrics, then observability as a designed property with an SLO attached.
The Cascade. One vendor outage takes down everything. Caching, async and circuit breakers, then resilience composition: backpressure, idempotency, honest degradation.

Part VI: The Architect

The Split. "Microservices by Q3." Bounded contexts, the strangler fig, sagas and the outbox, the modular-monolith defense: argued from both sides, on the record.
Faster. Idle threads burn money. Virtual threads vs reactive, native image, then runtime selection as a decision memo on cost per -ility.
The Architect's Chair. A vague spec, a final design review, a green pen changing desks. System design, the five debug drills, reading framework source and mentoring.

Capstone

The Hostile Review. Six months later, an acquirer's hired guns run a due-diligence architecture review. Kenza defends the whole system, every chapter's decision attacked in one room, and the reader sits the exam with her.

Part II: The Container

The nouns, before the story (plain prose; skip freely if you already run Spring)
Scope: how many instances of a bean exist. The default is singleton: one shared instance for the whole application, used by every request at the same time, so any field you put on a singleton is shared by every concurrent request at once.
Bean lifecycle: the fixed sequence the container walks for every bean: construct → inject dependencies → run init callbacks → wrap in proxies if needed → serve → destroy at shutdown.
BeanPostProcessor: container machinery that may inspect or replace each bean as it is built. Most "magic" annotations are implemented by one.
AOP proxy: a generated wrapper that runs logic around your method (open a transaction, check a permission). Calls reach your method through the wrapper. AOP stands for aspect-oriented programming: behavior that many methods need, such as a transaction, is written once and applied around them.
@Transactional: the annotation from Part I that puts a method inside a transaction. What this part adds: if the method throws an unchecked exception, the proxy rolls the transaction back, and nothing written inside it is kept.
Spring Data repository: the bean you call to load and save one kind of entity, such as ReportRepository. Its built-in methods, save() and findById() among them, join the transaction that is already open. When nothing has opened one, each call runs in a transaction of its own, which commits before the call returns.
Managed entity: an entity that the current session is tracking. Change a field of a managed entity inside a transaction and Hibernate writes the change to the database at commit, with no save() call. That check at commit is called dirty checking.
Auto-configuration: Boot's conditional defaults, meaning pre-written configuration that activates only when your classpath and properties say it applies.
Starter: a dependency bundle that pulls in one feature's libraries at tested, compatible versions.
Profile / configuration properties: named environment overlays (dev, prod) and typed objects bound from YAML or environment variables.

Chapter 4: The Magic Show
The failover drill was scheduled for 6:30 on a Tuesday morning in March, which meant Youssef had been awake since five, drinking coffee the consistency of roofing tar and narrating his own actions like a bomb-disposal video. The plan was boring on purpose: kill the Postgres replica in prod, watch the platform degrade gracefully, watch the dashboard go amber, watch the alert fire, bring the replica back, write down the timings. Atrium had survived seven years; the drill was supposed to confirm the folklore.
Youssef killed the replica at 6:31. Then he waited for the dashboard to notice.
It didn't. The health panel glowed the same serene green it had glowed all night. He refreshed it, then curled the actuator endpoint directly. It answered "status":"UP", smooth as a salesman. Meanwhile, two terminals over, the replica was (his word in the incident channel) extremely down. For forty minutes a real degraded dependency was invisible to every pane of glass the company owned, and the only reason anyone knew was that Youssef had broken it himself, on purpose, with a calendar invite.
At standup he projected two JSON payloads side by side, component details shown in both. Staging's health endpoint showed a db component, dutifully UP. Prod's showed Boot's stock components, diskSpace and ping among them, and nothing about a database: no db, no replica check. The top-level status was a green lie.
"Last week's platform dependency bump went out Thursday," Youssef said. "Version numbers only. Reviewed and approved." He did not look at Kenza. He didn't have to; she'd approved it herself. The diff had been green and the bump tidy, the kind of PR you wave through between meetings.
Rachid studied the two payloads for a long moment. Then he asked the room, mildly, "Why does this bean exist in staging and not in prod?"
Nobody answered. The room held eight engineers and seven years of folklore, and not one person could say why any given health bean existed anywhere.
"Then nobody owns it," Rachid said. He capped his pen. "Magic is just a mechanism you haven't read yet. Roadmap work is cancelled this afternoon. Bring lunch."
The investigation
Kenza started where she always started: grep. ReplicaLagHealthIndicator appeared nowhere in Atrium's source. It wasn't in config/ or monitoring/, or in any @Configuration class she could find. No code the team had written in this repository defined the bean that was supposed to watch the database.
At Meridian this would have been a line in main(), she thought. new ReplicaLagHealthIndicator(dataSource, maxLag), registered by hand: code I wrote, in a file I owned, that a dependency bump could not silently delete. The instinct that wiring lives in user code was exactly why she'd never thought to look anywhere else. This time the hand-wired reflex had been a blindfold instead of a head start.
The class lived in a separate internal repo: glasshouse-monitoring-spring-boot-starter, written in 2021 by an engineer who'd left in 2023. Inside was a small auto-configuration:
// glasshouse-monitoring-spring-boot-starter, migrated from
// spring.factories for Boot 3, imports patched for Boot 4;
// nobody read it either time.
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(ReplicaHealthProbe.class)   // compiled against osprey-metrics 2.x
@ConditionalOnProperty("glasshouse.monitoring.replica-probe.enabled")
public class ReplicaMonitoringAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    HealthIndicator replicaLagHealthIndicator(
            DataSource dataSource,
            @Value("${glasshouse.monitoring.replica-probe.max-lag:5s}") Duration maxLag) {
        return new ReplicaLagHealthIndicator(new ReplicaHealthProbe(dataSource), maxLag);
    }
}

Next to it in the repo sat a fossil: an empty META-INF/spring.factories with a three-year-old comment, moved to AutoConfiguration.imports for Boot 3, delete after merge. The actual registration now lived in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports, one fully-qualified class name on one line. That file was the bean's birth certificate, and nobody at Glasshouse had ever read it.
"Reproduce it," Rachid said. "Locally. Don't theorize."

⏸ Your call. Two conditions gate that bean; Thursday's bump changed only version numbers. Which gate failed in prod, why was the failure silent, and which -ility just died with the dashboard? Commit.

Kenza booted Atrium with the prod property set and --debug on the command line. The ConditionEvaluationReport filled her terminal: every auto-configuration Boot had considered, hundreds of them, with the conditions each had evaluated and the verdict. She scrolled past DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched, past Jackson, past Tomcat, hunting. Then:
ReplicaMonitoringAutoConfiguration:
   Did not match:
      - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class
        'io.osprey.metrics.jdbc.ReplicaHealthProbe' (OnClassCondition)

Youssef and two others had drifted over, and the room audibly exhaled. The dependency bump had taken osprey-metrics from 2.9 to 3.0. In 3.0 the vendor had repackaged: io.osprey.metrics.jdbc became io.osprey.metrics.probe.jdbc. The starter jar, compiled against 2.x, asked the classpath for a class that no longer existed at that address. And @ConditionalOnClass did precisely what it was designed to do: it backed off, with no ClassNotFoundException, no warning and no log line. Nothing had malfunctioned. The silence was the feature, pointed the wrong way.
(If you called @ConditionalOnClass at the pause, take the second beat too. The -ility that died wasn't availability: the replica was allowed to fail, and that was the drill. The casualty gets named at the Wall and billed to the supply chain.)
"That explains prod," Youssef said slowly. "Why did staging never catch it?"
Kenza pulled up the profiles. There it was, the second condition:
# application-prod.yml: the only place the module was ever switched on
glasshouse:
  monitoring:
    replica-probe:
      enabled: true        # staging never sets this: "staging has no replicas"

management:
  health:
    db:
      enabled: false       # 2021: "the custom check is better", and prod kept no fallback

Staging had never run the custom probe at all, because the activating property existed only in the prod profile. So staging fell through to Boot's default db health contributor. That check is a connection-validity ping, Connection.isValid() against the primary, and it knows nothing about replicas. Staging therefore showed a database check, just not the one prod depended on. And prod had been left with no fallback: the original author had disabled Boot's default there because the custom check was "better," so when the custom probe stopped registering, no database check remained at all. Both environments were green, and each was wrong in its own way.
Kenza stared at the enabled: false line and thought of the sinkhole Rachid had circled and dated in January: code is copied more often than it's read, inked beside a return type that leaked raw JPA entities across an API boundary. The note covered more than that one return type. It marked any working-but-wrong pattern that propagates by paste. Config was worse: yaml is copied with no compiler to object and no type to mismatch. This line had outlived its author by three years, and it had meant nothing to anyone who'd pasted profiles around it since.
"Two conditions and a profile," Rachid said. "A murder weapon in three parts. Now, to the Wall. All of you."
What the senior sees
Rachid drew two doors on the Wall, side by side, both opening into a box labeled ApplicationContext.
"Every bean enters through one of these. Door one." He tapped it. "Kenza, what's inside @SpringBootApplication?"
"It's…" She caught herself before saying the magic annotation. "Three annotations. @SpringBootConfiguration, which is a @Configuration, so the class can define beans, and which is the marker @SpringBootTest searches for. @ComponentScan, which walks downward from the main class's package. That's why AtriumApplication sits at com.glasshouse.atrium and everything lives beneath it. And @EnableAutoConfiguration."
"Door one is yours," Rachid said. "Your packages, your stereotypes, scanned from the root down. Move the main class and half your beans vanish, but at least they vanish loudly. Door two is the one nobody here had read." He wrote AutoConfiguration.imports over the second door. "Boot does not scan jars hoping to find configuration. It reads a list. Every jar may carry one file at META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. The import selector behind @EnableAutoConfiguration collects every such file on the classpath and gets a roll-call of candidate classes. Before Boot 2.7 the list lived in spring.factories, your fossil. A starter that still registers only there is silently dead on anything modern. Sound familiar?"
"Then the conditions," Kenza said. "A candidate still has to pass its gates."
"Name the gates."
"@ConditionalOnClass asks whether this type is on the classpath. The annotation itself is read from the class file's metadata with ASM, never loaded, which is why an auto-configuration can safely name a class that isn't there, and why its absence makes no sound. @ConditionalOnProperty asks whether the operator turned this on. @ConditionalOnBean and @ConditionalOnMissingBean ask whether the context already contains, or lacks, a bean." She paused, seeing the shape of it. "And those last two only make sense if there's an order. They're evaluated against the beans registered so far."
"Which is why ordering is part of the contract," Rachid said. "@AutoConfigureAfter, or the after attribute on @AutoConfiguration. Condition on a DataSource before DataSourceAutoConfiguration has run and your gate fails for a bean that was ten milliseconds from existing. And the back-off gate, OnMissingBean, is the whole social contract of Boot. Why does your @Bean beat Boot's default, every time, with no flag?"
Kenza worked it through aloud. "User configuration is processed before auto-configuration is evaluated. So when Boot's default DataSource bean reaches its @ConditionalOnMissingBean check, my bean is already in the registry. Boot sees it and yields. I win by declaring, not by disabling." She looked at the yaml still on the screen. "Which is what 2021-guy should have done, instead of turning the default db check off with a property and leaving prod with no net."
So a starter is a Maven dependency that arrives already wired, she thought. At Meridian a jar was just bytes on the classpath, and the wiring was always mine to write. This is dependencies plus the code that registers them, and the registration travels inside the jar. The naming convention got two minutes: glasshouse-monitoring-spring-boot-starter, company-first, because spring-boot-starter-* belongs to Boot itself. The parent BOM (bill of materials) got five. spring-boot-dependencies pins hundreds of third-party versions, tested together as one matrix. That was exactly why the bump of everything in the BOM had been safe, and why osprey-metrics, which wasn't, had walked in unread.
Rachid capped his pen. By now the team knew it meant the mechanism was settled and the bill was coming. "Name what this incident spent. Youssef."
"Operability. For forty minutes the system couldn't tell us the truth about itself."
"That's the symptom's -ility. Kenza, the cause's."
"Evolvability," she said, slower. "But not ours. The supply chain's. We treated Thursday's bump as a chore; it was an architecture event. The blast radius ran from osprey's jdbc package, through a condition in a starter nobody had read, into prod's only database health check. And the diff that detonated it was two characters of version number."
"Because the BOM is a contract," Rachid said. "Inside its tested matrix, a bump moves you between tested points. Outside, where osprey lived from the day it got its own version line, the testing burden is yours whether or not anyone signs for it, and the upgrade gets a reviewer who asks what the jar promises the classpath and which conditions, in which repos, lean on that promise." He nodded at the condition report still on Kenza's screen. "The second rule you've already run. The container will explain its own composition, every candidate with its gates and its verdict: --debug at boot, /actuator/conditions while it runs. A system you can interrogate is an operability property like any other. It exists only if you design the habit of asking. This morning the answer took four minutes to read and three years to think of reading."
Then Rachid drew a ladder on the Wall and labeled the rungs top to bottom: CLI args > env vars > profile yml > application.yml > defaults. He drew it low, under the lifecycle column and February's smoke cloud (the proxy drawn as a cloud around the raw bean; the advice lives on that wrapper, and a this. call never crosses it). The Wall now read like the container itself, first how a bean is born, then who decides whether it may be:


Resolution starts at the top: the first rung that defines a property wins. A lower rung speaks only when every rung above it stays silent.
"The other half of your murder weapon. A bean can be gated on configuration, and configuration is a layered fight. Higher rung wins. Youssef, prove the ladder."
Youssef, without ceremony, set GLASSHOUSE_MONITORING_REPLICA_PROBE_ENABLED=true on the staging deployment and let the pod restart. The env var outranked the profile file, and relaxed binding mapped the screaming snake case onto the kebab-case property without anyone writing a translation. The probe module woke up in an environment whose yml had never heard of it.
Meridian's homegrown loader had a crude version of this, Kenza thought. Read the properties file, then let -D flags stomp it: two rungs, hand-coded, in a class from 2014. This is the same ladder grown five rungs tall, with the case-translation I'd never have thought to write. For once the hand-wired instinct is a head start instead of a trap.
"One more thing," she said, and it came out before she'd decided to confess it. "At Meridian I wrote all of this wiring myself in main(), and I complained about the boilerplate constantly. Boot deleted the boilerplate, and I never once asked where it went."
"Every convenience is a debt of understanding," Rachid said. "Today you paid one back."
The fix
The rewrite was small and merciless. Every condition became explicit and carried a comment saying why. The property binding moved out of stringly-typed @Value into a validated record. The difference is mechanical. @Value resolves one string at one injection point and fails wherever that bean happens to live, while @ConfigurationProperties binds the whole tree: typed, relaxed, validated at startup, and visible to the IDE's metadata. And the starter's own bean now wore the back-off gate, so any future app could override it by declaring:
@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("glasshouse.monitoring.replica-probe")
public record ReplicaProbeProperties(
        boolean enabled,
        @DefaultValue("5s") @DurationMin(seconds = 1) Duration maxLag) { }

@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)  // the DataSource must exist first
@ConditionalOnClass(name = "io.osprey.metrics.probe.jdbc.ReplicaHealthProbe") // 3.x home, by name
@ConditionalOnBean(DataSource.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "glasshouse.monitoring.replica-probe",
                       name = "enabled", havingValue = "true")
@EnableConfigurationProperties(ReplicaProbeProperties.class)
public class ReplicaMonitoringAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(name = "replicaLagHealthIndicator")  // override by declaring
    HealthIndicator replicaLagHealthIndicator(DataSource ds, ReplicaProbeProperties props) {
        return new ReplicaLagHealthIndicator(ReplicaHealthProbe.of(ds), props.maxLag());
    }
}

The management.health.db.enabled: false line was deleted from the prod profile; Boot's default primary check now ran everywhere as the baseline, with the replica probe layered on top. The fossil spring.factories was finally buried. Because a silent absence had cost them forty blind minutes, Kenza added the test the incident had shown was missing: a startup smoke test that boots the context with prod-shaped properties and asserts, by name, that the critical beans exist. It says nothing about whether they work. Absence had just been promoted to a failure class of its own.
It was, she realized while naming the test class, ADR-002's move aimed at a new target. The fitness functions from the morning staging died politely had turned architecture rules into executable claims that fail the build the moment they stop being true; this one made the container's composition the same kind of claim.
The runbook gained its shortest and most useful page: "My bean didn't get created": run with --debug, read the ConditionEvaluationReport, find your class under negative matches, read which condition said no. The report is the answer; everything else is guessing.
One more file rode along in the PR, the binder's fourth entry, half a page, dated:

ADR-004: Config governance.
Context: A transitive repackage inside a routine version bump silently removed prod's only database health bean; at standup nobody could say why any bean existed anywhere. Decision: Feature configuration binds through typed @Validated @ConfigurationProperties only, with no raw @Value in feature code; profiles overlay a shared base, never fork it; every third-party version rides the BOM or gets a named owner; a startup smoke test asserts critical beans exist by name; reading the --debug condition report is a documented runbook skill. Consequences: Config becomes a schema, validated at boot; the BOM constrains upgrade freedom in exchange for a tested matrix; absence is now a failure class with a test that catches it.

⚖ Your move, architect
The PR was easy to approve. The harder decision sat underneath it: what is Atrium's config strategy, now that everyone has watched a bean vanish without a sound? You have seen what they chose. Before the reveal, say in one sentence why each of the other two options loses.

A. Fix the bean, keep ad-hoc @Value and tribal knowledge. Document the gotcha on the wiki; zero process cost today.
B. Govern it. Typed @Validated @ConfigurationProperties only, profiles that overlay rather than fork, all versions on the BOM, the bean-existence smoke test, condition-report reading as a runbook skill.
C. Centralize now. Stand up Spring Cloud Config Server: one source of truth, runtime refresh, every deployment pulls its config at boot.

The trade-offs, since you've committed: A costs nothing today and prices the next vanishing bean at a day of blind dashboards. The tribal knowledge it leans on resigned in 2023, and operability stays folklore. B is what Kenza wrote into ADR-004. It charges a schema tax (every knob needs a record, a constraint and a metadata entry) and buys interrogability: config that fails loudly at boot instead of lying silently at runtime, and bean existence asserted by a test instead of assumed from memory. C buys runtime refresh nobody asked for. The price is a new failure domain in front of every boot (config server down, fleet can't start), plus a consistency question nobody was ready to answer in March: which pods hold which config? The shape is the same as January's move. B keeps C purchasable, because typed records relocate to any backend, while C bought now is infrastructure in search of a requirement. (Chapter 14 prices central config honestly, once there's more than one deployable to feed.)
"Where does Kubernetes point at this thing, now that it's back?" Youssef asked, mostly to himself, while reviewing the PR. "Liveness, readiness, we should fight about that properly someday." Nobody took the bait. It was March; that fight was a September problem, and nobody knew it yet.
On Friday, Kenza gave her first-ever brown-bag, standing at the front of a room instead of the side of one. She titled the deck The Magic Show and walked the whole chain: @SpringBootApplication to its three annotations, the two doors into the context, the .imports roll-call, the conditional gates, and the precedence ladder Youssef had inked permanently onto the Wall beneath February's smoke-cloud proxy drawing and its caption, this. goes around the mirror. The penultimate slide was the one nobody had asked for and everybody photographed: the greenfield path, the same machinery with nothing on fire. New service → start.spring.io → pick the starters. The parent BOM pins every third-party version, so you declare dependencies and almost never a version number; auto-configuration conditions in a working baseline off your classpath. Your whole job is a typed @ConfigurationProperties record for your own knobs, an application-{profile}.yml per environment, and one calm read of the condition report before the first deploy.
Her closing slide was a single sentence: A bean is never magic. It is a list entry that survived its conditions.
Rachid sat in the second row and wrote nothing in green the entire hour. Afterward, he stopped at her desk and pointed his pen toward the controllers package.
"You know how the beans are born," he said. "Now learn what they do all day."
The debrief: Ch.4, The Magic Show
Say it first. Out loud, 90 seconds, before you read below the line.

Kill-shot 4. How does @EnableAutoConfiguration find configurations, and how would you debug one that didn't apply?

Then the follow-ups, cold:

Why does your own @Bean override Boot's default, and when doesn't it?
Why is @ConditionalOnBean dangerous without @AutoConfigureAfter?
The platform team proposes Spring Cloud Config Server "so this never happens again." Your call?
@ConfigurationProperties or @Value?
How do you write a custom starter?

Tick what you said:

☐ Claim: Boot never scans jars for configuration: it reads a declared list and lets conditions veto it.
☐ Mechanism: The AutoConfiguration.imports files, the @Conditional gates, and user configuration processed first so @ConditionalOnMissingBean defaults yield.
☐ Trade-off: Silent back-off lets your @Bean win without flags, and the price is that absence produces no error and no log.
☐ Failure mode: A renamed class or an unset profile property deletes a bean with zero output. --debug and the ConditionEvaluationReport show it.

Three ticks pass. With fewer, re-read the scene named in the story anchors and try again tomorrow.


The model answer. Claim: Boot never scans jars for configuration; it reads a declared list and then lets conditions veto it. Mechanism: @EnableAutoConfiguration imports a selector that reads every META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports file on the classpath (spring.factories before Boot 2.7/3.0), then evaluates each candidate's @Conditional gates: OnClass against ASM-read metadata so an absent class can't blow up the read, OnProperty against the environment, and OnBean/OnMissingBean against the beans registered so far, which is why @AutoConfigureAfter ordering is part of correctness. User config is processed first, so Boot's @ConditionalOnMissingBean defaults yield to your declarations. Trade-off: Silent back-off is the design. It is what lets your @Bean win without flags, and the price is that absence produces no error and no log. Failure mode: A renamed class or an unset profile property deletes a bean with zero output. The diagnostic is --debug (or /actuator/conditions) and reading the negative matches in the ConditionEvaluationReport. Grepping your own code finds nothing, because the bean was never in your code.

THE ARCHITECT'S LENS

-ilities at stake: Evolvability as a supply-chain property: the BOM is a tested-matrix contract. Bumps inside it move between tested points, and a dependency outside it makes every upgrade an architecture event with a blast radius someone must own. And operability as interrogability: a container that can explain its own composition (--debug, /actuator/conditions) gives you that property only if reading the explanation is a designed habit. Silent back-off spends operability to buy override-by-declaration; ADR-004 buys it back at the beans that matter.
The ADR: ADR-004, config governance: typed @Validated @ConfigurationProperties only, profiles overlay (never fork), versions ride the BOM or get an owner, critical beans asserted by name in a startup smoke test, the condition report a runbook skill. Config becomes schema, validated at boot.
Rejected alternatives: ad-hoc @Value plus tribal knowledge (free today; the next vanishing bean costs a blind day, and the tribe resigned in 2023); Spring Cloud Config Server now (runtime refresh nobody asked for and a new failure domain in front of every boot, re-priced in Ch.14); disabling auto-configuration and hand-wiring everything (fighting the whole social contract to punish one unread jar).
Fight or lean: Lean on conditions and the BOM: silent back-off is what lets your @Bean win by declaring, and the matrix is tested so you don't have to. Fight the silence wherever your 3 a.m. depends on a bean existing. The framework can't know which absences are fatal to you, so promote those to existence that a smoke test asserts by name.

Story anchors

The green dashboard over a dead replica → @ConditionalOnClass backing off silently after the class moved packages in a routine bump.
The two doors on the Wall → @ComponentScan from the root package (your beans) vs AutoConfiguration.imports (the jars' beans), two distinct entrances into the context.
Youssef's env-var flip on the staging deployment → the config-precedence ladder (CLI > env > profile yml > application.yml > defaults) plus relaxed binding mapping SCREAMING_SNAKE onto kebab-case.
Rachid's standup question, "Why does this bean exist in staging and not in prod?", met by eight engineers' silence → a bean nobody can explain is a bean nobody owns; ADR-004 turns existence into an asserted, smoke-tested claim.

Interview ammo

Kill-shot: How does @EnableAutoConfiguration find configurations, and how would you debug one that didn't apply? It reads the AutoConfiguration.imports files from every jar (not classpath scanning) and filters each candidate through its @Conditional gates. To debug one, use --debug//actuator/conditions and read which condition vetoed your class.
Follow-up: Why does your own @Bean override Boot's default, and when doesn't it? User config registers before auto-config evaluates, so Boot's @ConditionalOnMissingBean sees your bean and backs off. It fails to back off when your bean's type/name doesn't match what the condition checks, and then you get both.
Follow-up: Why is @ConditionalOnBean dangerous without @AutoConfigureAfter? Conditions evaluate against bean definitions registered so far, so without ordering you can condition on a bean that's defined ten milliseconds later and wrongly back off. Only condition on beans from configs you're explicitly ordered after.
Architect follow-up: The platform team proposes Spring Cloud Config Server "so this never happens again." Your call? Wrong -ility. This incident was about interrogability, not centralization. Typed validated properties plus a bean-existence smoke test buy that without a new failure domain in front of every boot. Central config gets priced when there are multiple deployables and a real runtime-refresh requirement.
Follow-up: @ConfigurationProperties or @Value? @Value resolves one string at one injection point and fails wherever that bean happens to live. @ConfigurationProperties binds the whole tree into one typed object, with relaxed binding, validation at startup and metadata the IDE can read.
Follow-up: How do you write a custom starter? Name it company-first, as in glasshouse-monitoring-spring-boot-starter, because spring-boot-starter-* belongs to Boot. Put the beans in an @AutoConfiguration class and list its fully qualified name, on a line of its own, in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. Make every condition explicit, order the class with after, bind its knobs through a @ConfigurationProperties record, and put @ConditionalOnMissingBean on its beans so an application overrides one by declaring its own.

part-03.html.body:
Part III: The Request

The nouns, before the story (plain prose; skip freely if you already run Spring)
Servlet: Java's standard unit of HTTP handling. All of Spring MVC runs as one servlet.
Filter: code that sees every request before (and after) the servlet runs. Security lives here, before your code is ever reached.
DispatcherServlet: Spring's front controller. It receives every request and routes it to the matching controller method.
Controller: the annotated class whose methods handle routes. Arguments are bound from the request, and validated only where the method declares it (@Valid on a body, a constraint on a parameter); return values are serialized to JSON by message converters.
Worker thread / pool: the embedded server (Tomcat) gives each request one thread from a bounded pool. While a thread is busy with one request, it serves no other.
Timeout: an upper bound you can set on how long an outbound call may wait.

ch-06.html.body:
Chapter 6: The Pool
The "Spring into Security" banner went live at ten o'clock on a Tuesday, and for twenty glorious minutes it worked as promised: sign-ups tripled. Leila stood at the back of the exec room watching the load balancer's traffic line, the only graph Atrium had, climb like a good quarterly slide.
At 10:31, Cortexa began answering in thirty seconds instead of three hundred milliseconds. This was the third-party CVE-enrichment vendor that Atrium called synchronously inside every report submission. Their status page would later say elevated latency in one region. Glasshouse's status page said nothing, because at 10:32 Glasshouse stopped saying anything at all.
The whole site 503'd. The submission form went down, and so did login, the leaderboard, and the static marketing page the promo pointed at, which was served through the same app. The brick screamed on the desk of whoever held it that week, and Youssef appeared at Kenza's shoulder, already having checked the obvious things.
"CPU?" Kenza asked.
"Six percent." He turned his laptop around: six healthy-looking pods, idling. "Memory's fine. Disk's fine. Postgres is bored. The site is down and every machine involved is having a restful morning."
In the war room, an exec said the sentence execs say: "Can we add more pods?" Youssef added more pods. Six became twelve became eighteen, and the traffic graph didn't move. The new pods came up green, accepted connections, and went exactly as silent as the old ones.
"We just bought more chairs," Youssef said, "in front of the same locked door."
Leila was on the bridge, watching launch conversions flatline in a window two executives could also see. "Someone tell me what the door is."

⏸ Your call. Idle CPUs, eighteen green pods, a site answering 503. Before the thread dump, name the exhausted resource, what's holding it, and which -ility is failing. Commit.

The investigation
Eight years of production Java at Meridian Freight said: find the exhausted resource, because something always is. CPU, memory, and database connections all checked out, so Kenza went looking for the resource nobody graphs.
She picked a pod and took a thread dump.
"http-nio-8080-exec-117" #341 daemon prio=5 RUNNABLE
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
        at sun.nio.ch.SocketDispatcher.read0(java.base/Native Method)
        at sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.implRead(java.base)
        ...
        at org.springframework.web.client.DefaultRestClient$DefaultResponseSpec.body
        at com.glasshouse.atrium.enrichment.EnrichmentService.enrich
        at com.glasshouse.atrium.report.ReportSubmissionService.submit

She grepped the dump. One hundred and ninety-six threads named http-nio-8080-exec-* sat in the same native socket read, all waiting on api.cortexa.io. None had crashed, and none was erroring. The JVM reports a thread blocked in a native read as RUNNABLE, which is its idea of a joke. Four workers were doing actual work. The rest were parked, each holding open a request the load balancer had long since abandoned.
(If you called the worker pool: right resource, and the right -ility is availability. Hold your fix; the napkin math is about to price it.)
She pulled up the code she'd walked past a dozen times without seeing:
@Service
public class EnrichmentService {

    // Built ad hoc years ago, on HttpURLConnection. No timeouts configured anywhere.
    private final RestClient cortexa = RestClient.builder()
            .baseUrl("https://api.cortexa.io")
            .requestFactory(new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory())
            .build();

    public CveEnrichment enrich(SubmittedReport report) {
        // Called synchronously from ReportSubmissionService.submit(...)
        return cortexa.post()
                .uri("/v1/enrich")
                .body(EnrichmentRequest.from(report))
                .retrieve()
                .body(CveEnrichment.class); // parks this Tomcat worker as long as Cortexa pleases
    }
}

A read blocks until it returns. That's just the network, she thought. It was the Meridian reflex, from eight years of raw sockets behind a hand-configured Jetty where a blocking read had never once cost more than its own wait. The model itself held no surprises. In Tomcat's default model, exactly as in the Jetty pool she had sized by hand, the thread is the request: one worker carries it from connector to filter chain to controller to this socket read and back. While Cortexa held the socket, that worker could do nothing else, and everything it carried waited with it. She had never set a timeout at Meridian either. No library had set one on her behalf, and the freight traffic had never made her pay for the omission. This morning Cortexa sent the invoice.
On the bridge, Youssef was explaining why the site hung instead of failing fast. "Tomcat's NIO connector keeps accepting sockets after the workers are gone, up to max-connections, eight thousand-odd by default. They sit with the poller, queued for a worker that's never coming back. Past that there's accept-count, a backlog of about a hundred. Past that, connection refused. And the probes and ingress health checks are HTTP requests too. They queue behind the same dead pool and time out, the pod drops from the Service, and the front door answers 503: no healthy upstream. Eighteen pods, declared dead for telling the truth too slowly."
Rachid had been silent in the corner of the war room. Now he spoke, mostly to the exec.
"The server didn't run out of CPU. It ran out of patience tokens. It has two hundred of them per pod, every request borrows one for its whole lifetime, and a vendor in another region is holding a hundred and ninety-six of them hostage, per pod. Kenza. Show them the math."
What the senior sees
Kenza took a napkin, because the Wall was three rooms away and the bridge was waiting.
"Little's law, informally: requests in flight equals arrival rate times how long each one takes. Each pod is taking about seven submissions a second right now. That's the promo working. Normally a submission takes three hundred milliseconds, so seven times zero point three is about two threads busy per pod. Trivial.
"Cortexa goes to thirty seconds. Same arrivals, hundred-times duration: seven times thirty is two hundred and ten concurrent, and the pool is two hundred. That's server.tomcat.threads.max, the default, untouched since this repo was created. The submission endpoint alone now demands more than the whole pool, so it absorbs all of it, and login and the leaderboard starve behind it. One slow downstream doesn't slow down one feature. In thread-per-request, it confiscates the threads every feature shares."
"And the pods?" the exec asked. "Eighteen is triple the capacity."
"It would be, if arrival rate were a constant, but it's a crowd. Every user staring at a spinner hits refresh, the load balancer re-sends what timed out, and demand climbs to meet whatever capacity we add. And every new pod opens hundreds more concurrent calls into a vendor that's already drowning. We're making Cortexa slower by scaling at it."
One mercy was January's: the eighteen pods had at least come up interchangeable. The whiteboard-bolted-to-the-kitchen-wall bug, the singleton stashing a draft on a field every thread shared, was the kind of state that breaks scale-out, because identical pods stop being identical. Statelessness had bought the right to scale out, and the pool was the next bottleneck up.
She drew the connector where it sat on the Request Journey, left of everything they'd traced on the Wall in March, when the team had walked one HTTP request from socket to database and back. Socket → connector → filter chain → DispatcherServlet → onward. Nothing on March's line was failing: the filters were idle and the DispatcherServlet barely entered, because a request only reaches them on a worker thread, and no workers were free. The outage lived in the Journey's first box, drawn as a single word and never opened. "Everything we traced last month happens on a worker thread. The connector is the toll booth where the thread gets assigned, and we've never once looked at it, because Boot embedded it and it worked."
She sketched the rest on a second napkin, transcribed that evening onto the Wall, under the Journey's far-left box:


Under it, the law in one line: in-flight = arrival rate × residence time.
"Run it backwards," Rachid said from the doorway.
Kenza flipped the napkin. "Pool fixed at two hundred, residence thirty seconds: two hundred divided by thirty. Six point six requests a second, per pod, for everything."
"That's the postmortem's first line. As of this morning, availability is division, and division forces a design question: how much of the pool may one dependency hold? Today, all of it. A bulkhead, a small pool per dependency, makes that a number somebody chose. Size it stingy and it rejects honest traffic, so the number is a negotiation. Blast radius is a design property, and we never designed ours."
At Meridian she had built the server inside the app by hand, an embedded Jetty wired line by line in main(), so Boot's fat jar (java -jar and the server comes up with the code) was the one part of Spring she had trusted from day one. Atrium's pom.xml even had a war profile from the years when it deployed into a standalone Tomcat. That was the old order, where the server owned the app instead of the app carrying its server. The profile had been dead since the move to Kubernetes, kept around like an appendix.
Someone on the bridge asked the perennial question: "Is Tomcat the problem? I've read Jetty is faster."
Rachid looked at Kenza. She shook her head. "Swapping is one starter exclusion: drop spring-boot-starter-tomcat, add spring-boot-starter-jetty, and Boot's ServletWebServerFactory auto-configuration wires whichever container is on the classpath. Undertow used to be the third door. It's off the menu as of Boot 4.0; it never caught up to the Servlet baseline. And it would change nothing, because the servlet model is the model: one thread per in-flight request, bounded pool. We'd be renaming the pool. The problem is that we let a thirty-second stranger borrow our threads with no return date."
"There is a structural answer," Rachid added quietly. "The JVM grew threads that stop being precious, cheap enough that blocking one is nearly free. That conversation is worth having." He checked his watch. "Not at eleven twenty, mid-incident, in front of finance." He wrote virtual threads, later in the napkin's corner; that corner would wait until November.
Two seconds or thirty
Mitigation came first: Youssef flipped Cortexa enrichment off behind a config property, the parked threads drained as their socket reads finally returned, and the site came back in ninety seconds. The exec left. Then came the argument about what normal should be.
Kenza proposed timeouts: one second to connect, two seconds to read, on every outbound call Atrium made, starting with Cortexa.
Leila pushed back hard, and she wasn't wrong to. "Researchers wait for those scores. Enrichment is half of why submission feels smart. So if Cortexa has a slow afternoon, we just... fail it?"
"Today Cortexa had a slow morning and we failed everything: login, leaderboard, your launch. The trade-off isn't enrichment-works versus enrichment-fails; it's one feature degrading honestly versus the whole site degrading dishonestly. A timeout is us deciding in advance how much of our capacity a vendor may hold."
"Then don't make the researcher wait at all," Leila said, and that, everyone agreed afterward, was the actual fix. If enrichment could fail without failing the submission, it shouldn't be inside the submission. Accept the report, commit it, return 201, and enrich afterward; the score appears when it appears.
Leila lost the argument she'd started and won the one that mattered. Kenza was learning that this is what a good trade-off discussion looks like.
The fix
The timeouts went in as policy. As of Boot 4.0, the spring.http.clients.* properties set connect and read timeouts for every client built through Boot's auto-configured RestClient.Builder. That gave Atrium a global floor, committed to application.yml before any named client got its own numbers:
spring:
  http:
    clients:
      connect-timeout: 2s   # the global floor: a forgotten client may be slow,
      read-timeout: 5s      # never unbounded; named clients override stricter

The Cortexa client then chose stricter numbers, with a name attached:
@Configuration
class CortexaClientConfig {

    @Bean
    RestClient cortexaClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
        var settings = HttpClientSettings.defaults()
                .withConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
                .withReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));
        return builder
                .baseUrl("https://api.cortexa.io")
                .requestFactory(ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder.detect().build(settings))
                .build();
    }
}

The numbers had a derivation, because Rachid asked for one. "Where does two seconds come from?"
"The submission route promises four seconds at p99," Kenza said. "Our own work spends about half a second: Postgres, serialization, the filter chain. Connecting to Cortexa may spend one more. What's left is what guests may borrow. Two seconds is Cortexa's share of a budget, not a mood."
"Then the budget goes next to the route," Rachid said. "Budgets nobody can see get spent twice. And when Leila wants the timeout raised, and she will, that's a product negotiation over who gets the missing second." The Request Journey, it turned out, was also a ledger, with every hop spending from the same four seconds.
By evening the ledger entry sat where reviewers would trip over it, in two comment lines above the mapping. ADR-006 would make that convention house style:
// Route budget (ADR-006): POST /api/v2/reports promises p99 4s
//   = ours 0.5s + connect 1s + Cortexa 2s + headroom 0.5s; raising a share is a product call
@PostMapping(version = "2")
ResponseEntity submit(
        @Valid @RequestBody SubmitReportRequest request) { /* ... */ }

Later that week the enrichment call moved out of the request path, and its three seconds came off the budget comment above the route. submit() now persisted the report and recorded enrichment as pending. A background worker on a small, bounded, named executor called Cortexa afterward and filled in the score. A two-second timeout on a deferred call costs a retry, where the missing timeout on the inline call had cost a launch.
Then came the connector itself, configured deliberately for the first time in seven years. The numbers were mostly the same, but now they were decisions instead of dust:
server:
  shutdown: graceful           # the default since Boot 3.4, pinned explicitly
  http2:
    enabled: true              # multiplexes streams; NOT more workers
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200                 # the pool: hard ceiling on concurrent requests
      min-spare: 10
    max-connections: 8192      # sockets the NIO poller will hold open
    accept-count: 100          # backlog once max-connections is full
    connection-timeout: 5s     # slow/idle clients can't squat on a connection
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s   # the drain window: how long "finish" gets

Graceful shutdown hadn't needed enabling (it has been Boot's default since 3.4), yet the mid-incident rolling restarts had still killed in-flight requests, an error spike on top of the outage. Graceful only waits out the drain window before abandoning what's left. Threads parked thirty seconds on Cortexa outlived it. What was new was that window, timeout-per-shutdown-phase, now a number somebody owned. SIGTERM still meant stop accepting, finish what you hold, then die. Youssef scheduled a drill against the cluster's preStop hooks, because he does not believe YAML until he has watched it. HTTP/2 got a one-line caveat in the commit message: multiplexing reduces connection pressure, not thread pressure; every request still borrows a worker.
"Deploys are availability events," Youssef said, taping the drill date to the Wall. "One real outage a year, forty deploys a quarter. Get the drain window wrong and the deploys are the outage, sliced thin." The runbook gained one line in Kenza's hand: the drain window must outlive your slowest in-flight request, or graceful is a longer word for kill. Youssef added the other bound under it: the window also has to fit inside the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds, which defaults to 30 seconds and starts counting before the preStop hook runs, so a 30-second drain needs a longer grace period in the pod spec.
The deploys got faster too. Every image build had been shipping the 200-megabyte fat jar as one Docker layer. The Dockerfile now ran java -Djarmode=tools -jar atrium.jar extract --layers --launcher, splitting dependencies, loader, and application code into separate layers. A one-line change now shipped kilobytes instead of the world, and mid-incident that difference is minutes.
Kenza wrote the decision note that afternoon, three sentences long: Every outbound call gets a timeout. Every timeout gets a named owner who chose the number. Someday this call gets a circuit breaker: a timeout decides how long one request waits; something still needs to decide when to stop sending requests at all. That last sentence was a promissory note that came due in September. By the time it reached the binder, the note had grown a number:

ADR-006: The latency budget.
Context: One slow vendor consumed every worker thread in a bounded pool; the whole site 503'd with CPUs idle. Decision: Every outbound call carries an explicit timeout derived from a per-endpoint latency budget; budgets sum along the Request Journey and are recorded next to the route; no unbounded waits anywhere, with spring.http.clients.* as the global floor. Consequences: Slow dependencies now fail fast and partially instead of globally, and degraded modes become explicit product negotiations. This is the Leila conversation, institutionalized: every new dependency starts with an argument about its share of the budget.

⚖ Your move, architect
Rewind to 11:20, with the site down, finance in the room, and the mitigation flag not yet found. The capacity question had three honest answers. You have seen what they chose. Before the reveal, say in one sentence why each of the other two options loses.

A. Raise threads.max and keep adding pods. No code change, and it is visible action: the exec is already nodding.
B. Queue-and-async the vendor call. Enrichment never belonged in the request path; accept, commit, return 201, enrich later.
C. Timeouts plus a per-dependency bulkhead, now. Cap how long any request may wait on Cortexa and how many may wait at once; config and one small bean.

The trade-offs, since you've committed: A spends cost to buy minutes, not availability. Eight hundred threads at 30 s residence are just eight hundred parked threads; retries raise the arrival rate to meet whatever capacity you add; and every new pod ships its own Hikari pool, opening fresh connections against a Postgres that had no part in this outage (that bill arrives in Chapter 9). B is the right shape for the long term: Chapter 13 builds it properly, with a bounded queue, retries, and idempotency, and Chapter 14 makes it durable. Mid-incident, though, it is a redesign wearing a fix's clothes, and it spends operability exactly when the team has none to spare. The deferred worker shipped that week was a first step toward B, affordable once C had made failure cheap. C is what the team chose: it buys availability by capping blast radius at the slow dependency, so Cortexa's worst afternoon now costs an enrichment outage while the rest of the site stays up. The price is hard conversations with Leila about what "degraded" shows users, and those conversations are a feature. C is a bridge that buys the quarter: the structural answer to the economics of blocking a thread arrives in November as ADR-015's virtual threads.
A backlog ticket appeared, titled "Real application metrics: we graphed the LB because we had nothing else," filed with no sprint attached, where it began to age. And Kenza walked over to Youssef's desk and put her name on the on-call rotation.
"You sure?" he said. "The brick doesn't care what you were doing at three a.m."
"I stood in a war room today and the only person with evidence was me. I'd rather be the person with evidence."
Youssef considered the thread dump still open on her laptop. It was the first time, he told Rachid later, that a developer had brought him evidence instead of vibes. He slid the rotation spreadsheet across.
The debrief: Ch.6, The Pool
Say it first. Out loud, 90 seconds, before you read below the line.

Kill-shot 6. How does the thread-per-request model work, and how does one slow downstream take a whole Spring Boot service offline?

Then the follow-ups, cold:

Would swapping Tomcat for Jetty, or adding pods, help?
What do threads.max, max-connections, and accept-count each bound?
How do you pick a timeout that isn't a guess?
Where do you set the connect timeout and the read timeout?
What happens on SIGTERM under graceful shutdown?

Tick what you said:

☐ Claim: Thread-per-request: each request occupies one thread of a bounded worker pool (200 by default), so the pool is the concurrency ceiling.
☐ Mechanism: The connector hands each request to a worker, a blocking call parks it, and Little's law prices it: arrival rate × duration.
☐ Trade-off: Simple and debuggable, with real stack traces, but request duration is partly other people's systems: capacity is hostage to your slowest dependency.
☐ Failure mode: One slow downstream consumes the entire pool, health probes starve, pods get marked down, and the whole site returns 503 while CPU idles.

Three ticks pass. With fewer, re-read the scene named in the story anchors and try again tomorrow.


The model answer. Claim: Boot's default embedded Tomcat is thread-per-request: a bounded worker pool (200 by default) where each request occupies one thread for its entire lifetime, so the pool, not CPU, is the concurrency ceiling. Mechanism: The NIO connector accepts sockets (up to max-connections, with an accept-count backlog behind that) and hands each ready request to a worker. Every blocking operation in the handler, such as JDBC or a synchronous RestClient call, parks that worker until it returns, and Little's law prices it: threads needed ≈ arrival rate × request duration. Trade-off: The model is simple and debuggable, with real stack traces and no async contagion, and the bounded pool is a crude built-in load shed. But request duration is partly controlled by other people's systems, so your capacity is hostage to your slowest dependency. Failure mode: One downstream going from 300 ms to 30 s multiplies one endpoint's thread demand a hundredfold and consumes the entire pool. Health probes starve in the same queue, pods get marked down, and the whole site 503s while CPU idles. Adding pods just parks more threads against the same dependency. The first defense is a timeout on every outbound call; the structural fixes are circuit breakers or virtual threads.

THE ARCHITECT'S LENS

-ilities at stake: Availability, revealed as arithmetic: a bounded pool divided by residence time is the throughput ceiling, and residence belongs to your slowest dependency until a timeout takes it back. Blast radius sits on top: bulkheads exist to keep one dependency's failure down to a feature outage. Operability rides along. The drain window is availability at the end of the lifecycle, because deploys are the most frequent availability events a system has.
The ADR: ADR-006, the latency budget: every outbound call carries a timeout derived from a per-endpoint budget; budgets sum along the Request Journey and live next to the route; no unbounded waits anywhere.
Rejected alternatives: scale-out under fire (multiplies parked threads, vendor pressure, and DB connections; that bill arrives in Chapter 9); swapping Tomcat for Jetty (renames the pool, keeps the model); full queue-and-async mid-incident (the right shape at the wrong hour; Chapter 13 builds it properly).
Fight or lean: Lean on Boot's connector defaults and the spring.http.clients.* global floor: the numbers are sane, and the floor catches the client somebody forgot. Fight the silence around defaults: nobody had read threads.max: 200, so nobody had decided on it, and it sat as dust for seven years until a vendor priced it.

Story anchors

196 of 200 threads parked in the same socket read on cortexa.io → thread-per-request exhaustion: workers are the scarce resource, and the CPU sits idle.
"We just bought more chairs in front of the same locked door" → horizontal scaling can't outrun a slow dependency: new pods' threads park too, and retries raise the arrival rate.
The napkin: 7/s × 30 s = 210 > 200 → Little's law: concurrency demanded = arrival rate × duration, and the pool is the ceiling.
The flipped napkin: 200 threads ÷ 30 s ≈ 6.6 req/s → availability run backwards: pool divided by residence time is the pod's throughput ceiling, whoever owns the residence.

Interview ammo

Kill-shot: Explain how a single slow third-party API can 503 your entire Spring Boot service while CPU sits idle. Each request holds one of ~200 Tomcat workers for its full duration. When a downstream stretches duration to 30 s, arrival rate × duration exceeds the pool and every worker parks in a socket read. New connections queue at the poller until health checks fail and the load balancer drops the pods. That is thread exhaustion, with the CPU idle.
Follow-up: Would swapping Tomcat for Jetty, or adding pods, help? No. The swap (exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat, add the Jetty starter; Boot wires whichever ServletWebServerFactory is on the classpath; Undertow is gone as of Boot 4.0) changes the container and keeps the blocking servlet thread model. More pods just multiply parked threads against the struggling vendor. The fixes are outbound timeouts, deferring the call, circuit breakers, or virtual threads.
Follow-up: What do threads.max, max-connections, and accept-count each bound? threads.max caps concurrent in-flight request processing. max-connections caps sockets the NIO poller holds open (cheap while idle: keep-alive connections don't hold workers). accept-count is the listen backlog once connections are full; beyond it, refusals.
Architect follow-up: How do you pick a timeout that isn't a guess? Derive it from a latency budget: the route promises a p99, subtract what your own hops spend, and the remainder is the most any dependency may borrow. Record it next to the route, give it a named owner, and renegotiate it as a product decision when someone wants it raised.
Follow-up: Where do you set the connect timeout and the read timeout? In two places. spring.http.clients.connect-timeout and spring.http.clients.read-timeout are the global floor for every client built from Boot's auto-configured RestClient.Builder (2 s and 5 s at Atrium). A named client overrides them with HttpClientSettings.defaults().withConnectTimeout(...).withReadTimeout(...), handed to its request factory: the Cortexa client gets 1 s to connect and 2 s to read.
Follow-up: What happens on SIGTERM under graceful shutdown? The server stops accepting new requests, finishes the ones it holds, then exits. server.shutdown: graceful has been Boot's default since 3.4. The wait is capped by spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, the drain window (30 s here): whatever is still running when it ends is abandoned, so the window must outlive the slowest in-flight request and fit inside the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

Part IV: The Data

The nouns, before the story (plain prose; skip freely if you already run Spring)
Persistence context: the map of entities Hibernate watches during a transaction. It caches by identity, detects your changes by diffing snapshots (dirty checking), and writes them at commit.
Lazy loading: a fetch strategy. An association is loaded on first access rather than up front.
N+1: a query pattern. One query loads a list, then one more runs per element as each is touched.
Transaction: the all-or-nothing unit of work, opened and committed by a proxy around an annotated method. Propagation: how nested calls share (or suspend) it. Isolation: what concurrent transactions are allowed to see of each other.
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking: optimistic locking detects a conflicting write at commit via a version column, and you retry or surface it. Pessimistic locking blocks other writers with a database lock while you hold the row.
Repository: an interface Spring Data implements at runtime; method names and annotations define the queries.
Projection: fetching exactly the columns a view needs into a record, instead of loading whole entities.
Migration: versioned, append-only SQL scripts (Flyway) that evolve the schema. Connection pool: the small fixed set of database connections (Hikari) every request must borrow from.
