Chapter 13: The Cascade
The first thing Kenza noticed, at 2:14 on a Tuesday afternoon in late September, was that she could see it.
The Grafana board, built out of the 3 a.m. postmortem's shame, showed submission p99 climbing like a fever chart, and outbound calls to Cortexa, the CVE-enrichment vendor, timing out in red stripes. Their synthetics had alerted eleven minutes before the first researcher tweet. After nine months of debugging by flashlight, the lights were on.
Rachid was on planned leave: a cabin, a lake, deliberately no signal. Whatever happened next was Kenza's.
On the war-room screen, Youssef overlaid two graphs: Cortexa's status page (investigating elevated load in EU region) and Glasshouse's outbound rate to cortexa.io.
"Their status page says elevated load," he said. "We are the elevated load. We're sending them three times our organic traffic."
Kenza found it in four minutes. April, when the whole site 503'd waiting on this vendor, had ended with timeouts on every outbound call and a decision note in her handwriting: someday this call gets a circuit breaker. Someday never came. The sentence had ridden into ADR-006's margin as a promissory note, and today it came due. What came instead, in a commit labeled temporary, was this:
// EnrichmentService, "temporary" since April
ReportEnrichment enrich(String cveId) {
    for (int attempt = 1; attempt 
Three attempts, back to back: no backoff, no jitter, no budget. Every failing call became three, so a regional outage tripled Glasshouse's outbound traffic against a vendor already failing. Inside Atrium, each enrichment tied up a thread for nine seconds of stacked timeouts instead of three. It was Little's law again: in-flight equals arrival rate times residence, so tripling residence tripled the threads held. Pools filled, and the backlog spread into unrelated paths until the tracker itself slowed. It was April's pool exhaustion wearing a distributed coat: Cortexa, already drowning, held underwater by its own customer.
"First move is triage, not architecture," Kenza said, steadier than she felt. "Kill the retries behind the feature flag. Right now we are part of their DDoS. We stop being that, then we design under calm."
The flag flipped; within minutes the outbound graph dropped to organic levels and Cortexa's status page began, slowly, to recover.
The investigation
The retry storm explained the cascade's force. It did not explain its reach. Submission was supposed to survive Cortexa entirely: April's other fix was submit now, enrich later, an @Async hand-off to a background executor. So why was the report-detail page, a pure read path, timing out?
Imane asked the fatal question. "Wait. Isn't enrichment cached? Why are we calling them at all on the detail page?"
She pulled up her own cache panel: cve-enrichment hit rate, a flatline at zero, flat since the day the dashboards went up. The bug was older than the measurement: her refactor, mid-August.

⏸ Your call. A @Cacheable that compiles, runs, and returns correct data, with its hit rate flat at zero since an August refactor. Commit before Imane scrolls: what's wrong, and which -ility has been quietly uninsured?

The room went quiet the way it had in February, when it was Kenza's own name on the commit. Imane scrolled to the code and found it:
@Service
public class EnrichmentService {

    private final CortexaClient cortexaClient;   // constructor-injected

    public ReportEnrichment enrichmentFor(Report report) {
        return this.fetchEnrichment(report.cveId());      // ← the bug
    }

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "cve-enrichment")
    public ReportEnrichment fetchEnrichment(String cveId) {
        return cortexaClient.fetch(cveId);
    }
}

"It compiles," Imane said slowly. "It runs. It returns the right data. It has just… never cached anything. Every detail view, straight to the vendor, and nobody noticed because Cortexa is fast when it's healthy."
(If you called it at the pause: the mechanism is February's, a this. call that never crosses the proxy. The -ility is not performance. The cache was availability insurance against exactly this afternoon, and its premium lapsed without a test going red.)
Kenza fetched a printed postmortem from her desk: February, her own name in the author line. PM-32: Half-saved triage states. Root cause: @Transactional method invoked via this., bypassing the proxy. It was the same mechanism. The annotation's behavior lives in the proxy the container hands your callers, and a this. call dispatches on the raw object behind it, so the interceptor never runs. ADR-003 had made this a named review finding, and the August review read past the line. February's ghost, back in a new coat.
"I shipped this exact bug in February," she said, handing it over. "Different annotation, same mirror. Let me show you the smoke cloud." In January it had been a printed diff in green ink on Kenza's desk. Now it was a printed postmortem on Imane's, the same treatment passed down.
February's proxy drawing was still on the Wall: the smoke cloud in front of a box labeled your actual object, the caption faded but legible: this. goes around the mirror. Kenza re-inked every line and added a list underneath: @Transactional · @Cacheable · @Async · @PreAuthorize: same mirror, same trap. Rachid had said that as a warning, and it took seven months to come true.
At Meridian a retry was a for-loop you could see, the old voice observed. Crude, and wrong in three other ways (no backoff, no budget, no breaker), but impossible to walk around. Here, the annotation is a promise only the proxy keeps.
What the senior sees
"Say the mechanism back to me," Kenza said, and heard, mid-sentence, whose cadence she was borrowing.
"Spring's annotation-driven features aren't compiled into my class," Imane said. "At startup, a BeanPostProcessor sees the annotation and wraps my bean in a proxy, a CGLIB subclass here. The proxy holds the interceptor: check the cache, open the transaction, dispatch to the executor, then call my code. External callers get the proxy from the container. But inside my own class, this is the raw object. The call never crosses the proxy boundary, so the interceptor never runs. Nothing is broken. It's bypassed."
"And that's the scary part," Kenza said. "It fails silently and correctly. The unit test passes, because the method returns the right value. Only a hit-rate graph could catch it. Yours did; code review didn't."
She sketched the incident as a stack of absences:
Timeouts were the foundation, and the only layer that covered every call. Without April's timeouts (ADR-006, the latency budget), every request thread would have blocked on the unanswering vendor until none remained: the thread-pool funeral, rerun. But a timeout bounds one call. It says nothing about how many you make.
Retries without a budget multiply load on a struggling dependency. A retry is a bet that the failure was transient. It needs exponential backoff so attempts spread out, and jitter so a thousand clients don't synchronize into waves. Three immediate retries against a regional outage bet nothing: they only add load to something already failing.
Nothing remembered that Cortexa was down. Every request rediscovered the outage from scratch and paid the full timeout each time. That's the circuit breaker's job. Kenza drew the state machine next to the smoke cloud. Closed: calls flow, failures counted in a sliding window. Past a failure-rate threshold it opens: calls fail fast, with no thread consumed and no vendor touched. After a wait, half-open admits a few probes: if they heal it closes, and if they fail it snaps open. The breaker is the system's memory of recent pain.
Nothing isolated the blast on the read path. April's bulkhead was the small executor behind submission, and it covered that path only. The detail page called Cortexa on request threads, the pool every other page draws from, so a sick optional feature starved a healthy critical one. A bulkhead, a hard cap on concurrent enrichment calls, turns "Cortexa is down" into "enrichment is down," and nothing more.
"Fourth tool in that kit," Youssef said. "Rate limiter." Kenza added it. A rate limiter is a ceiling on outbound rate, enforced even when everything is green: the breaker reacts to their failures, the bulkhead caps our concurrent calls, and the rate limiter bounds what we send in the first place. "This morning's flag was a rate limiter set to zero, by hand." She penciled the numbers beside it:
resilience4j:
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      cortexa:
        limit-for-period: 50
        limit-refresh-period: 1s
        timeout-duration: 0

Fifty permits per one-second window. timeout-duration: 0 means the fifty-first call fails fast instead of queueing up to dogpile the next refresh. The breaker protects you from a failing dependency. The rate limiter protects them, and your contract, from you, which is why it holds even when every graph is green.
And the async path lied about its own health. April's @Async enrichment executor was bounded in threads only: nobody had set a queue capacity, and ThreadPoolTaskExecutor defaults it to Integer.MAX_VALUE. Under the storm it accumulated forty thousand pending tasks while showing eight busy threads and no errors. Meridian's hand-rolled executor hid its backlog exactly this way, Kenza thought. Same lie, older clothes. An unbounded queue converts overload into silent latency and creeping memory instead of a signal.
"One more," Youssef said. "Retries mean some calls land twice: they process our request, die before answering, we send it again. Anything that retries is at-least-once; the far side has to absorb duplicates."
"Idempotency key on every enrichment call," Kenza agreed. "Keyed by the CVE, same as the cache, so the same request twice is a no-op on their side. And write the rule down: at-least-once arrives with your first retry, not with a broker someday. Idempotency is the precondition for every retry-shaped tool on this Wall. The durable version (write the intent in the same transaction as the data, deliver later, dedupe on the consumer) is the outbox pattern. We'll need it the day anything splits out of Atrium." She underlined it twice, not knowing how soon.
The fix
They designed under calm. The fix was February's pattern reused verbatim: when an annotation needs a proxy boundary, extract the bean. The vendor boundary became one small class whose only job was to be called from outside itself:
@Component
public class CortexaGateway {   // the resilience boundary

    private final RestClient cortexa;   // connect 1s, read 2s

    public CortexaGateway(RestClient cortexaRestClient) {
        this.cortexa = cortexaRestClient;
    }

    @Retry(name = "cortexa")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "cortexa")
    @Bulkhead(name = "cortexa")
    public ReportEnrichment fetch(String cveId) {
        return cortexa.post().uri("/v1/enrich")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", "enrich-" + cveId)
                .body(new EnrichmentRequest(cveId))
                .retrieve()
                .body(ReportEnrichment.class);
    }
}

The three annotations come from io.github.resilience4j:resilience4j-spring-boot4, the Resilience4j starter built for Boot 4. They are aspects, so spring-boot-starter-aspectj sits beside it in the POM: without that starter the application still starts, nothing wraps the gateway, and all three annotations do nothing.
The verb was April's, unchanged. Cortexa enriched by POST, so the method offered no idempotency for free, and the key had to build it. The key is what makes this POST safe to repeat, and that construction, not the verb, is what licenses the @Retry stacked above it. A GET wouldn't have needed the header; every retried write on this Wall does. Kenza spelled it out in the PR description, because "retry only idempotent calls" gets read as a scavenger hunt when it's a construction project.
In front of it: EnrichmentCache, fifteen lines, constructor-injected, its single method wearing @Cacheable(cacheNames = "cve-enrichment", sync = true) and delegating straight through. Two beans, two proxies, every call crossing both. The hit-rate graph moved within an hour.
Imane asked the sharp review question: why not a fallbackMethod on the breaker, returning the pending badge? Kenza pointed one layer up. "Anything returned underneath the @Cacheable gets cached. Breaker opens, fallback says pending, cache stores pending, and we serve 'pending' for a full TTL after Cortexa heals. The fallback lives above the cache, or the cache launders the lie." So EnrichmentService caught the failure above the cache and returned ReportEnrichment.pending(cveId): explicit, visible, never stored. A load that throws caches nothing.
The numbers lived in configuration, tunable without a deploy:
resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      cortexa:
        max-attempts: 3
        wait-duration: 500ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2.0
        ignore-exceptions:
          - io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.CallNotPermittedException
          - io.github.resilience4j.bulkhead.BulkheadFullException
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      cortexa:
        sliding-window-size: 50
        minimum-number-of-calls: 20
        failure-rate-threshold: 50
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 50
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 5
        ignore-exceptions:
          - io.github.resilience4j.bulkhead.BulkheadFullException
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      cortexa:
        max-concurrent-calls: 16

Jitter rode along as a review note: a randomization factor on each wait, via Resilience4j's interval functions, so a fleet of pods doesn't retry in synchronized waves. Slow calls counted against the breaker on purpose: a timeout that "succeeds" is still pain.
Ordering got its own Wall sketch, because Kenza nearly got it wrong. By Resilience4j's default aspect order, Retry sits outside the breaker. Each attempt passes through the breaker and is counted. Once the breaker opens, remaining attempts fail instantly with CallNotPermittedException, which the retry ignores, so an open breaker ends the storm instead of feeding it. Flip the nesting and three attempts look like one call. The storm hides inside the breaker's statistics. "Same annotations, opposite system," she wrote. "Ordering is semantics, not style." She drew the composition on the Wall:


They kept the default order on purpose, the why written underneath: the bulkhead takes a permit per attempt, so the cap holds mid-storm; ADR-006's timeout prices one attempt's worst case. One consequence of that order went into the YAML: a full bulkhead throws BulkheadFullException back out through the breaker and the retry, so both ignore lists name it, and a call refused by our own cap is neither counted as a vendor failure nor retried.
The cache triggered the afternoon's best argument. Imane wanted Redis: shared, durable, one cache for all pods. Kenza made her argue both sides. Caffeine is in-process: nanosecond reads, no network hop, nothing new to fail. But every pod warms its own copy and there's no shared eviction. Redis buys sharing at the price of a round-trip, serialization, and one more thing on the 3 a.m. dashboard. CVE enrichment is slow-changing, harmless to duplicate and fine to lose, so Caffeine with a TTL won, with Redis kept for the day they needed shared eviction. Refreshes went through @CachePut, which executes the method and overwrites the entry. A manual re-run hit @CacheEvict. And sync = true earned its one-breath defense: a hot key expiring makes every concurrent request miss at once and stampede the backend, and sync lets one caller per key load while the rest wait, per pod.
The executor kept its name, and its queue got a bound:
@Bean(name = "enrichmentExecutor")
TaskExecutor enrichmentExecutor() {
    var executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    executor.setThreadNamePrefix("enrich-");
    executor.setCorePoolSize(8);
    executor.setMaxPoolSize(16);
    executor.setQueueCapacity(200);   // bounded: overload becomes a signal, not a secret
    executor.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());
    return executor;
}

They argued the rejection policy aloud. CallerRunsPolicy was tempting (backpressure for free) until Kenza traced it: under overload, the request thread runs the enrichment, synchronously, against a sick vendor. April, reinvented by a constructor argument. AbortPolicy won. The @Async("enrichmentExecutor") submission point catches the rejection, the report keeps its pending badge, and a @Scheduled sweeper re-enqueues once the breaker closes. One caveat went on the PR: Boot's default scheduler is single-threaded unless you size it, so a slow sweep delays every other job. An AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler went in beside it: a void @Async method that throws never reaches its caller, and by default it's merely logged by a handler nobody watches. Theirs fired an alert.
Kenza capped the marker on a line written under the smoke cloud: backpressure is a system property, not a queue setting. "Every bound (pool, queue, retries, bulkhead) is the system saying no while no is still cheap," she said. "Unbounded anything is deferred failure. Availability isn't surviving load; it's refusing the load you can't survive."
Which left the badge. Leila fought it, because that was her job. "Researchers see 'severity pending enrichment' and read 'broken.' Synthesize a medium severity while Cortexa's down. Smooth it over."
"A fallback that lies is an incident you've scheduled for later," Kenza said. "Severity drives bounty math. The day our invented 'medium' turns out to be a critical, we're explaining money, not a badge. The fallback degrades honestly: what we know, what's coming, nothing invented. What a user sees while we're failing is a contract, and product co-signs it." Leila held the stare, then nodded, the same nod she'd given on timeouts in April. The badge shipped, researchers barely noticed, and trust held. Fallbacks that degrade honestly entered the house style that week.
⚖ Your move, architect
The badge settled new, never-enriched reports. The harder question outlived the incident: what should the detail page show for reports enriched weeks ago, when Cortexa goes dark and cache entries age out? Leila brought renewal numbers: an hour of erroring detail pages reads as "the platform is down." Malika brought trust: her triagers act on severity and must know how far to trust the page. Three policies went up on the Wall. Commit before reading on.

A. Fail fast, visibly. Breaker open → the panel says so. Honest, simple, nearly free, and triage stops entirely for the duration.
B. Queue-and-drain. Accept everything, enrich eventually, show pending meanwhile, and build the durable queue now.
C. Serve the last known enrichment, marked STALE with its age. "Enriched 41h ago · vendor degraded." The cache becomes a record of history as well as an accelerator.

The trade-offs, since you've committed: A spends availability to buy simplicity and perfect honesty. Leila's renewal argument killed it on the record: a vendor's bad hour promoted to a triage outage is the cascade re-implemented as product policy. B is the right shape for writes: it's the outbox pattern Chapter 14 builds. Mid-incident it's a redesign, and reads can't queue: a triager looking at a report now can't be handed a ticket number. C shipped, buying availability with a named freshness tax: the cache kept entries past their freshness window, anything stale carried an age stamp, and the failure mode was decided in advance. Stale under 48 hours is actionable, older escalates to manual, and first-contact CVEs keep the pending badge. Leila's renewals and Malika's trust resolved on the record: the degraded view is a designed product contract, where before it was whatever the exception handler left on screen.
The record went into the binder before the week was out, the longest entry yet, with the most scars to cite:

ADR-013: Resilience composition.
Context: A Cortexa regional outage met an unbudgeted retry loop ("temporary" since April); our outbound tripled, pools filled, and the cascade reached unrelated paths, while an August @Cacheable had never cached once (self-invocation, again). Decision: The composition order is law: timeouts under everything (ADR-006 is the floor); bounded, jittered retry only on idempotent calls, every attempt crossing the breaker so an open breaker ends the storm; a bulkhead caps concurrent calls per dependency; a rate limiter wherever the contract demands one; every external call carries an idempotency key; fallbacks degrade honestly (pending or stale-marked with age, never fabricated); async work rides bounded, named executors. Consequences: A failing dependency now costs its feature, not the site; the price is configuration that must be load-tested rather than guessed, and a review rule: a bare retry loop is a finding.

The closed incident
Rachid came back Thursday, sunburned and unhurried, to a folder on his desk: timeline, postmortem, ADR-013, Wall photos, and the minutes of a review Kenza had run with Cortexa's engineers, with both companies' graphs on one screen and both sides' retries on the table. A closed incident, end to end, commanded by someone else.
He read it all, walked to her desk, and said only: "Who flipped the flag?"
"I did. Triage first. Architecture after."
He nodded once, the smallest nod she'd ever seen carry that much weight, and went to study the re-inked smoke cloud.
The only shadow: the CTO had read the postmortem, come away glowing about one word, resilience, and had a conference to attend in October. Next month's problem.
The debrief: Ch.13, The Cascade
Say it first. Out loud, 90 seconds, before you read below the line.

Kill-shot 13. How do you stop a failing downstream dependency from cascading through your service, and what goes wrong when the pieces are composed badly?

Then the follow-ups, cold:

Why do @Cacheable/@Async silently no-op on self-invocation?
Retry inside or outside the circuit breaker: what changes?
Why is an unbounded @Async executor queue dangerous?
Compose timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead, and rate limiter for one flaky vendor: what order, and why?
Walk the circuit breaker's three states, and say what each number in its configuration decides.
Can you retry a POST?

Tick what you said:

☐ Claim: A timeout, a bulkhead, a circuit breaker, a bounded retry on idempotent calls only, and a fallback that degrades honestly.
☐ Mechanism: What a timeout and a bulkhead bound, the breaker's closed, open and half-open states, and the retry outside the breaker.
☐ Trade-off: The price is configuration that must be load-tested, and a stale view with its age that product has to co-sign.
☐ Failure mode: A bare retry loop triples traffic against a failing vendor, and a flipped nesting hides the storm in the breaker's statistics.

Three ticks pass. With fewer, re-read the scene named in the story anchors and try again tomorrow.


The model answer. Claim: You compose five things in a fixed order: a timeout under every outbound call, a bulkhead, a circuit breaker, a bounded retry on idempotent calls only, and a fallback that degrades honestly. Mechanism: a timeout bounds one call and says nothing about how many you make; a bulkhead is a hard cap on concurrent calls; a circuit breaker counts failures in a sliding window while closed, opens past a failure-rate threshold so that calls fail fast with no thread consumed and no vendor touched, then goes half-open after a wait and lets a few probes close it or reopen it; a retry needs exponential backoff and jitter, sits outside the breaker so that every attempt is counted and an open breaker ends the retries, and is safe only on idempotent calls, which for a POST takes an idempotency key. Trade-off: a failing dependency now costs one feature while the site stays up; the price is configuration that must be load-tested rather than guessed, and a degraded view that product has to co-sign: the last known enrichment, marked stale with its age, buys availability with a named freshness tax. Failure mode: a bare retry loop with no backoff and no budget turns every failing call into three: an outage triples your traffic against a vendor already failing and stacks nine seconds of timeouts on each thread. Flip the nesting and the breaker sees three attempts as one call, so the storm hides inside its statistics.

THE ARCHITECT'S LENS

-ilities at stake: Availability under dependency failure. Resilience is availability on somebody else's worst day, composed, not installed: backpressure decides what the system refuses, idempotency what it may safely retry, honest degradation what users see while it fails. Taxes paid knowingly: operability (tunables that must be load-tested, one more 3 a.m. dashboard) and cost (per-pod caches, idle bulkhead permits).
The ADR: ADR-013, resilience composition: timeouts under everything (ADR-006 the floor), bounded jittered retry only on idempotent calls with every attempt crossing the breaker, bulkhead per dependency, rate limiter where the contract demands it, idempotency keys, honest fallbacks, bounded executors.
Rejected alternatives: the bare three-attempt loop (a multiplier aimed at a drowning vendor); fallbackMethod beneath the cache (the cache launders the lie for a full TTL); CallerRunsPolicy (April reinvented: a sick vendor's latency on request threads); synthesized severity (an incident scheduled for later); queue-and-drain mid-incident (Ch.14's outbox bought early, and reads can't queue).
Fight or lean: Lean on Resilience4j's annotations and default aspect order at a dedicated gateway bean: proxy wrapping is why the container is worth inhabiting, and Retry-outside-breaker is the correct semantics. Fight every default that hides failure: the unbounded executor queue, the logged-and-forgotten AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, any annotation whose effect you haven't seen on a graph.

Story anchors

Imane's flatlined hit-rate graph → @Cacheable behind a this. call: the proxy trap generalizes to every annotation-driven feature
"We are the elevated load" QPS overlay → retry storms: retries without backoff, jitter, and a budget are a self-inflicted DDoS on a struggling dependency
The "severity pending enrichment" badge → fallbacks must degrade honestly; a fallback that invents data is an incident scheduled for later
Leila's renewals vs Malika's trust, resolved on the record → the degraded view is a designed product contract; ADR-013 made stale-marked truth house law

Interview ammo

Follow-up: Why do @Cacheable/@Async silently no-op on self-invocation? Same mechanism as @Transactional: the behavior lives in a proxy interceptor created at postProcessAfterInitialization, and this. never crosses the proxy. Extract the annotated method into a separate injected bean. Nothing fails, because the method still returns correct results and the tests pass; only a flatlined hit-rate graph shows the misses.
Follow-up: Retry inside or outside the circuit breaker: what changes? Resilience4j's default puts Retry outermost: the breaker counts every attempt and, once open, fails the rest fast (have the retry ignore CallNotPermittedException); inverted, the breaker sees three attempts as one call and the storm hides from its statistics.
Follow-up: Why is an unbounded @Async executor queue dangerous? It turns overload into silent latency and memory growth instead of backpressure. Bound the queue, pick the rejection policy deliberately (caller-runs pushes a sick dependency's latency onto request threads), graph the depth, and register an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler so void async failures alert instead of just logging.
Architect follow-up: Compose timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead, and rate limiter for one flaky vendor: what order, and why? Timeouts under everything to price one attempt; bounded jittered retry only on idempotent calls, each attempt crossing the breaker (open = storm over); bulkhead caps what you'll spend waiting; rate limiter protects their contract even when green. Flip the nesting and the storm hides inside the breaker's statistics.
Follow-up: Walk the circuit breaker's three states, and say what each number in its configuration decides. Closed: calls flow, and failures are counted in a sliding window of the last 50 calls, with at least 20 recorded before the breaker judges. At a 50% failure rate it opens, and calls fail fast with no thread consumed and no vendor touched. After 30 seconds it goes half-open and admits five probes: if they heal it closes, and if they fail it opens again. A call that takes longer than two seconds counts as slow, and a 50% slow-call rate opens the breaker too.
Follow-up: Can you retry a POST? Only after you make it idempotent. A retried call can land twice: the far side processes the request, dies before answering, and receives it again, so anything that retries is at-least-once. The gateway sends an Idempotency-Key header keyed by the CVE, which makes the same request twice a no-op on the vendor's side, and that key is what licenses the @Retry. A GET would not have needed the header.

Part VI: The Architect

The nouns, before the story (plain prose; skip freely if you already run Spring)
Bounded context: a part of the domain with its own model and its own language. It is the natural unit to split along, if you ever split.
Modular monolith: one deployable whose internal borders are real enough to cut later. Strangler fig: evolving a system by routing traffic at the edge to new code, which grows while the old code starves.
Outbox: write the outgoing event in the same database transaction as the data, then relay it afterward, so that "saved" and "announced" can never disagree.
Saga: a cross-service flow built from local transactions plus compensating actions, because distributed transactions across services are not a real option.
Virtual threads: cheap JVM threads that release their OS carrier while blocked, which gives thread-per-request semantics without the pool ceiling.
Reactive (WebFlux): event-loop concurrency with explicit pipelines. It has the highest ceilings, and it is a different programming model with its own discipline.
Native image: compiling the application ahead of time into a binary. You get near-instant start and low memory, and you pay for them at build time.

Chapter 17: The Hostile Review
The Wall had an exhibit number now.
Legal's photographer had shot it panel by panel for the data room: the lifecycle column, the smoke cloud, the breaker's three states, eight years of DO NOT ERASE filed under GLASSHOUSE-TECH-047. Forty-seven again, Kenza had thought. The universe kept its accounts in green ink.
The rumor from December's QBR notes had a name now: Castellan, an enterprise security conglomerate whose customer list read like a banking regulator's holiday card. It also had a process, due diligence. Finance got a week and Legal got two. The architecture got one day, and Castellan sent hired guns to spend it.
"Amina," the lead said, shaking hands like she was returning something. "I read your decision records last night. All sixteen." A beat. "It's why we only need a day." Her partner, Mounir, introduced himself with a spreadsheet open. He priced everything in run-rate and risk, and was usually right to.
They were not villains, just the outside world doing professionally what @sable had been doing for free: testing the claims, in writing.
The ADR binder sat on the conference table: the printed trail, ADR-001 through ADR-016, tabbed and dated, January's half-page about feature seams on top. Kenza sat across from it, six months a principal architect, the green pen in her shirt pocket because today it was coming along. Imane sat at the end with a laptop, officially the note-taker. Rachid was advisory now, which meant he was somewhere with no meetings; his only contribution would arrive at day's end, two lines long.
"Here's the shape of the day," Amina said. "I won't audit your code. Your code is fine; code usually is. I'm going to attack your decisions. Defend them or reopen them; both are acceptable answers. Only one thing fails this audit." She didn't say what.
The gauntlet
She started with the oldest decision and the newest insult.
"A modular monolith. In 2027." Amina laid ADR-001 and ADR-014 side by side. "Every other target we've assessed this year showed our client a service catalog. You show me a folder of reasons not to have one. Defend not splitting."

⏸ Your call. Before Kenza answers: what's the defense that isn't nostalgia, and which -ility does the monolith protect? Commit; this chapter is your exam too.

"The seam decides, not the year," Kenza said. "Atrium is one deployable with enforced internal boundaries: feature packages have kept their internals package-private since ADR-001, and an ArchUnit rule has failed the build on every crossed dependency since January. One seam proved real, and that was Notifications: async by nature, no shared transactions, its own scaling shape. We extracted exactly that, on outbox rails, with idempotent consumers and one trace ID across all four hops. The price of staying together is one pager, one deploy pipeline, one set of ACID commits, and no independent scaling anywhere we haven't measured the need. And what service catalogs leave off the slide is that triage, payouts, and programs share transactions and a chatty schema. Cut there and every payout becomes a saga run by eleven people, a distributed monolith doing badly, in public, what one commit does silently for free."
"Or," Amina said, "you lacked the organizational muscle to split, and wrote a justification afterward."
Kenza turned ADR-014 around and pushed it across the table. "Then read the exit criteria, written before the split argument: we split a seam when it crosses no transaction, has its own scaling profile, and can staff its own on-call. Notifications met all three; nothing else does yet. The day one does, this document tells my successor to reopen it. That's the difference between a defense and a justification: a defense names the conditions under which it stops being true."
(If you committed at the pause: the -ility is evolvability. Enforced seams keep the split purchasable; the service catalog spends it up front on every boundary, real seam or not.)
Amina flipped to tab seven. "Next. You disabled open-in-view and now hand-write a projection for every screen. ADR-007 is very proud of this. From outside, it reads as fighting your framework. Teams that patch their platform usually don't understand it. Why should Castellan trust one that overrides its own foundation's defaults?"

⏸ Your call. Draft the answer that proves fighting the default was understanding it, and name the -ility OSIV was silently spending.

"Because we fought it on the record, with the mechanism in hand, which is the opposite of not understanding it," Kenza said. "Open-in-view keeps the Hibernate session, and the pooled connection under it, open across response rendering, so lazy loads during serialization succeed. Two consequences follow. Every missing fetch plan still works, so it ships as a hidden N+1. And request threads keep holding database connections after the transaction has ended, just to write JSON. We have an incident for each. The first is the twenty-eight-second dashboard in front of Northbeam's CISO: four hundred and one individually flawless queries, one for the page, then two lazy loads per row, four hundred in all. The second is the April outage, where nearly two hundred threads per pod sat parked behind one slow vendor, holding things they didn't need. It's the same shape, one layer down. Trade-off: a DTO type per view, the mapping tax paid forever. Failure mode of the default: the exception disappears in development and the pool drains in production." She tapped the binder. "We lean on Boot everywhere the default's bill is one we'd pay anyway. The ADRs are silent there, because silence means lean. We've fought exactly the defaults whose bill we'd already paid in incidents, and each fight has a tab. A fought default without a record is a patch; with a record, it's architecture."
"Hm." Amina flipped forward. "Tab eight. Optimistic locking on triage. Your concurrency strategy ships errors to users. A 409 is a failure you designed in and documented like an achievement." She was looking past Kenza, down the table. "You. You worked on the merge flow. Do you agree your users should see errors?"

⏸ Your call. A designed-in 409, attacked by a professional. Defend it in four beats, and name precisely what the alternative corrupts. Then watch who answers.

Imane closed the laptop halfway, which Kenza would later describe as the sound of a torch being passed.
"Yes, and I can show you why," Imane said. "Claim: optimistic concurrency is correct wherever contention is rare and hold time is human. Mechanism: a version column rides every update, UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = ?, and zero rows updated means someone got there first; the second writer gets a 409 and a refreshed view instead of a green toast. Trade-off: a visible conflict a handful of times a month against an invisible lost update. We've had eleven conflicts since January, every one retried inside a minute. Failure mode: the alternative had a body count before we changed it. Two triagers, same report, both saves succeeded, both got green toasts, and a five-thousand-dollar severity decision belonged to whoever clicked second. The pessimistic version just relocates the cost: a row lock held across a human coffee break is a queue with a database in it. We chose the error you can see over the corruption you can't."
Amina wrote down the last sentence. Kenza watched her do it and said nothing at all, because the proof of succession is that you don't have to.
The concessions
After lunch, Amina stopped circling.
"Tab ten. Your tokens." She read from her notes; the ADR she had memorized. "Stateless JWTs, fifteen-minute access tokens, refresh rotation. Which means that for an offboarded employee, a stolen laptop, a compromised researcher token, your platform cannot revoke a credential; it can only wait. Castellan sells to banks. Their offboarding clauses are measured in seconds, and their auditors ask for the mechanism, not the average."

⏸ Your call. Two answers exist here: the defense and the concession. Which does this room need, and which -ility has moved under the decision?

"The decision was right when we made it, and I'll defend that version first," Kenza said. "Statelessness was chosen deliberately, after a researcher token reached an admin endpoint and came back 200 OK with a bank's payout configuration. That token was authenticated but never authorized; no role check stood between it and the handler. The mechanism: every request is verified in the filter chain (signature against cached JWKs, issuer, audience, expiry) before the DispatcherServlet ever runs, and there is no server-side session store to operate or to protect. The trade-off went up on our Wall the same week: a stolen token stays valid until it expires; statelessness cuts both ways. We priced that window at fifteen minutes against year-one Glasshouse. The ADR records the heavier options, denylist and live introspection, as the day-two path, each buying back control by selling statelessness."
She walked to the real Wall, not exhibit 047, and uncapped the green pen.
"And you're right. The threat model under that decision just changed owners. Fifteen minutes was priced against our risk; under your customer base it's mispriced, and ADR-010 has named day two since July. So I'm declaring it." She wrote, high on the blank stretch beside the January column: ADR-017 candidate, revocation: jti denylist in the bearer filter. "Mechanism: every token carries a unique ID; the filter checks it against a shared denylist before the request proceeds. Entries expire with the TTL of the token they ban, so the set stays bounded. Cost: one lookup per request, and a policy decision nobody gets to dodge. Fail open and revocation silently vanishes whenever the store blips; fail closed and the denylist joins the availability budget. We'll fail closed and pay for it."
Mounir looked up, mildly interested, like a man watching someone volunteer for a tax.
Amina moved on without comment. "Tab fifteen. You bet the runtime on virtual threads, a JDK feature that spent two releases in preview before anyone would stand behind it. Pinning, a young ecosystem, and your p99 contract with Northbeam riding on it. Defend the bet."

⏸ Your call. Defend the bet, and name the evidence you'd put on the table.

"Final in 21," Kenza said, "September of 2023, three years before we flipped the flag. But the age wasn't the bet; reversibility was. We ran the bake-off in staging under Gatling at twice peak load, and we didn't trust the release notes about pinning, so we measured it: -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads, then JFR, with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned for threads that park while pinned and jdk.JavaMonitorEnter for threads kept waiting at a monitor. The recordings pointed at two offenders. A 2018 signing utility serialized every caller through one shared digest; its synchronized became a ReentrantLock, which a virtual thread parks on cleanly. A vendor SDK we couldn't edit was contained on a named sixteen-thread platform executor, because a platform thread that blocks is a budgeted cost, while a pinned carrier (a virtual thread that blocks without unmounting, welding itself to the platform thread beneath it) takes that capacity from every other virtual thread in the JVM. The pinning audit is a standing check rerun at every JDK upgrade. Newer runtimes keep retiring the synchronized pin, which we verify on ours and never assume, so the risk shrinks as the bet ages. And the bet was survivable because the programming model never changed: still thread-per-request, same stack traces, same ThreadLocal semantics. Rollback is a property flip and a pool-sizing exercise. The binder holds one-way doors we walked deliberately, records attached; this wasn't one. We bet a setting. Reactive would have bet the codebase, a one-way door through every signature, for backpressure we don't have a queue deep enough to need."
"Adequate," Amina said, which Kenza understood by then to be her highest grade, and nodded to Mounir.
Mounir turned his laptop around. "My turn. Circuit breakers, bulkheads, named executors, an outbox relay, a gateway, synthetic probes. I've priced your resilience stack in engineer-months and annual run-rate, and the number is on this screen. You process four hundred reports a week. This is over-engineering for your traffic."

⏸ Your call. Price the stack yourself before Kenza does: which pieces trace to a named incident with a postmortem attached, and, by Youssef's rule (he doesn't believe YAML until he has watched it), what would you cut? Commit; Mounir is about to find Glasshouse's.

"Resilience isn't priced against throughput," Kenza said. "It's priced against correlated failure, and ours was total, twice. The April outage: nearly two hundred Tomcat threads per pod parked in NioSocketImpl.implRead behind one slow vendor, CPUs idle, the whole site 503ing on launch day. Our traffic was modest; the blast radius was everything. In thread-per-request, a slow downstream doesn't slow a feature; it confiscates the threads every feature shares. That outage bought the timeout policy, ADR-006: a global floor, so a forgotten client can be slow but never unbounded. The September cascade bought the rest, ADR-013. Our own retry loop hit a failing vendor three times per request, no backoff, adding load at the worst possible moment, while a @Cacheable that had never cached a single entry sent every read straight to them. That was February's proxy ghost wearing a new coat: the annotation lives on the container's proxy wrapper, and a this. call dispatches on the raw object behind it, so the call never crossed the proxy and the annotation never ran. The breaker records recent failures and stops calls to a downstream that keeps producing them; the bulkhead turns the vendor is down into enrichment is down and nothing more. Every component on your screen traces to a named incident with a postmortem, which makes the stack insurance with the claims history attached."
Mounir nodded, conceding the column, then scrolled. "Then explain page forty-one of your runbook. Brownout tiers: under sustained saturation, shed enrichment, digests, leaderboard, in that order. Dated the week after that September cascade. Which drill validated it?"
Kenza opened her mouth, and closed it, and the silence did the arithmetic for everyone.
"None," she said. "It's been scheduled twice and eaten by roadmap twice. The flags exist. The tiers have never been shed in anger or on purpose."
"Then it isn't a capability," Mounir said, not unkindly; he was only pricing. "It's a hypothesis with a logo."
"It's worse than that," Kenza said, already walking to the Wall, "because undrilled flags rot. There's the flag that flips nothing since a refactor renamed the property, and the low tier that turns out to share a connection pool with the core path it was meant to protect. You discover those at 3 a.m. during the real brownout, and we know how that goes from the week Kubernetes restart-looped perfectly healthy pods over a database check wired into liveness instead of readiness, a ninety-second blip reading as a dead pod." She wrote the second line under the first: ADR-017 candidate: run the brownout drill. Untested designs are hypotheses. The ink was still wet when she sat back down. "That one's free, Mounir. You found it; we'll run it."
At five o'clock Amina closed the binder and squared it on the table.
"This morning I said only one thing fails this audit," she said. "It's defending everything. Most systems we assess are defended: by personality, by tenure, by whoever talks longest. Almost none are evidenced. You'll have our report in two weeks." She glanced once at the two wet lines of green on the Wall. "Leave those up."
Ten days later the report reached the CTO, and everyone quoted the same sentence from it. The strongest signal in this engagement, stronger than any single decision, is that the architecture has a mechanism for being wrong: two findings conceded in the room, priced on the spot, and owned before we left the building. An architect's authority, it turned out, was the trail of priced decisions plus the demonstrated ability to reopen one: defensibility as a body of evidence with a working appeals process.
⚖ Your move, architect
There are two ADR-017 candidates on the Wall, the audit adrenaline is fading, and integration planning starts Monday. The remediation priority is a real fork. Commit before reading on:

A. Close the revocation gap first. Security; enterprise sales pressure; the report's headline finding.
B. Run the brownout drill first. Operability; two afternoons and a staging cluster; the cheapest finding to retire, and the one that pages you.
C. Sequence both into the acquisition's first-90-days plan, with owners and dates attached.

The trade-offs, since you've committed: by now you can price your own bias. A optimizes for the -ility with a lobbyist and starves the one with a pager; B does the reverse, and reads to the acquirer as ignoring their headline finding. The team chose C, because the architect's move is never picking a favorite -ility; it's sequencing with names attached. And C has a price tag, said out loud in the room: the acquirer's headline security finding stays open for the better part of ninety days as a known revocation gap, dated and watched, under the scrutiny of the very people who wrote it. The room accepted that as cheaper than a panicked denylist that fails open, and Castellan, reading owners and dates instead of promises, accepted it too. The drill ran in week three: Youssef, two afternoons. One flag flipped nothing, exactly as Kenza had guessed. The second finding nobody had guessed: the shed order itself was wrong, with digests carrying a transitive dependency on enrichment, so that tier one couldn't shed without taking tier two down with it. Both were found at 1× load instead of at 3 a.m. The denylist went spike-design-ship across the ninety days, Imane's spike first, fail-closed from day one. Both lines lived in the integration plan where Castellan could watch them move. If you chose A or B, you were right about the work and wrong about the job.
Tab seventeen joined the binder that week:

ADR-017: Findings of the June architecture audit.
Context: Due-diligence review upheld the decision trail but surfaced two mispriced decisions: the JWT revocation window (ADR-010's recorded day-two path, now due under the acquirer's enterprise threat model) and a brownout design that has never been drilled. Decision: Add a fail-closed jti denylist in the bearer filter, its entries expiring with their token's TTL and its store added to the availability budget (Imane, 90 days); run the brownout drill as a quarterly gameday, first run within 30 days (Youssef). Consequences: We sell back a slice of statelessness and two afternoons a quarter; we buy revocation measured in seconds instead of TTLs, a rehearsed degradation mode, and a trail that demonstrably reopens, which the audit priced higher than any single decision in it.

One more item rode in on Monday's integration call, dressed as small. Castellan's analytics team wanted Glasshouse's report events flowing into their platform, and their lead made it sound like a favor to grant cheaply: "Just point your outbox topic at us; we'll adapt to whatever shape it has. Fully reversible, it's only a feed. Turn it off any time."
⚖ Your move, architect: name the door first
This fork has two questions, and the first one is the exam. Chapter 16 named the skill; nobody in this meeting is going to label the door for you. First commit to a classification, one-way or two-way. Then choose:

A. Publish the internal event schema as-is. Fastest; zero translation code; "reversible," per the man who asked.
B. Publish a versioned external contract. A purpose-built event shape behind a translation layer, the internal model free to keep moving behind it.
C. Decline streaming for now; ship a quarterly batch export while the integration relationship settles.

The trade-offs, since you've committed: classification first. The feed looks two-way, a topic you can switch off, but the schema inside it is one-way: the day Castellan's dashboards parse your internal event shape, that shape freezes. Your domain model now changes at the speed of someone else's backlog, and "turn it off any time" decodes to "break their dashboards any time," which an acquisition makes career-adjacent. The transport, meanwhile, is genuinely two-way: stream, batch, cadence, all renegotiable next quarter without breaking anyone. So the trap is misclassification, in either direction. A treats a one-way door as reversible: commit later means migrating later, under a live external contract, at twice the price and half the leverage. C over-commits caution on the part that was cheap to reverse. It burns a quarter of integration goodwill guarding the transport, which was never the risk. B is what went in the plan: a mapping class and a versioning policy, the same anti-corruption move ADR-014 bought at the Notifications border (a translation layer so another context's model can't reach your domain), pointed outward this time. Grade yourself on the classification, not the letter: if you named the schema one-way and the transport two-way, the choice followed by itself. If you picked B while calling the whole thing two-way, you got the right answer the way a coin does.
The office emptied around seven. The email arrived at 7:14, two lines, no greeting, and Kenza could hear the green ink in it:

Heard you conceded twice in front of the buyers. Good. An ADR you can't reopen is just dogma with a date on it.
Tell Imane the chair suits her too. R.

She didn't forward it; some things you deliver in person. The January column had six months of ink in it now, the audit's two findings drying beside it, and she took the green pen and ruled a fresh blank column on the far side, for whatever year two decided to be under new owners.
Imane appeared at her shoulder, reading the empty column. "What goes in it?"
"Whatever breaks next," Kenza said, and capped the pen. "Same two questions, every time. Show me the mechanism. And tell me which -ility it spends."
The debrief: Ch.17, The Hostile Review
Say it first. Out loud, 90 seconds, before you read below the line.

Kill-shot 17. What makes an architecture defensible under hostile review?

Then the follow-ups, cold:

An auditor attacks a decision you now believe is wrong. What do you do?
How do you retrofit revocation onto stateless JWTs, and what does it really cost?
What distinguishes an over-engineered resilience stack from a priced one?
Which production incident of your own would you bring to this room?

Tick what you said:

☐ Claim: A body of evidence: decisions priced in -ilities, recorded with rejected alternatives, plus a mechanism for reopening them.
☐ Mechanism: Every contested decision traces to an ADR (-ility bought, alternatives lost, conditions for revisiting), and each defense is grounded in named incidents.
☐ Trade-off: The trail costs a permanent writing tax and makes you precisely attackable. That precision lets a concession raise credibility.
☐ Failure mode: An architecture defended by tenure and talking with no records, or a trail treated as scripture with no appeals process.

Three ticks pass. With fewer, re-read the scene named in the story anchors and try again tomorrow.


The model answer. Claim: A defensible architecture is a body of evidence: decisions priced in -ilities, recorded with context and rejected alternatives, plus a demonstrated mechanism for reopening any of them. Mechanism: every contested decision traces to an ADR naming what was true at the time, which -ility was bought, which alternatives lost, and the conditions for revisiting; each defense then runs claim → mechanism → trade-off → failure mode, grounded in named incidents. The auditor attacks the decision and meets the record, not the personality. Trade-off: the trail costs a permanent writing tax and makes you precisely attackable, since a written decision can be refuted in a way folklore can't. But that precision is what lets a review end in two findings instead of a turf war, and lets a concession raise credibility where it would otherwise spend it. Failure mode: two mirror-image deaths: an architecture defended by tenure and talking (no records, every question re-litigated from memory), and a trail treated as scripture (records, but no appeals process; the team that defends everything fails the audit on the one question that mattered).

THE ARCHITECT'S LENS

-ilities at stake: Defensibility, the -ility above the others, which the whole book has been building toward: architecture as a body of evidence, where every -ility purchase has a receipt that names its return conditions. Beneath the two concessions are security (a revocation window priced against a threat model that changed owners) and operability (an undrilled degradation design is a hypothesis, not a capability), both reopened because the trail recorded them as reopenable.
The ADR: ADR-017, the audit's findings sequenced into the first-90-days plan: a fail-closed jti denylist and a quarterly brownout gameday, each with an owner and a date. It is the trail's first entry written in front of outsiders.
Rejected alternatives: defending everything (the trail as scripture, the one answer Amina said fails the audit); quietly fixing the JWT gap before the report landed (retires the finding but forfeits the signal: being wrong in public was worth more than the fix); re-litigating each attack from memory and charisma (personality-based architecture: wins mornings, loses acquisitions).
Fight or lean: the year's whole pattern, compressed for the witness stand: lean on the platform wherever the default's -ility bill is one you'd pay anyway (the ADR binder stays silent there, because silence means lean); fight only on the record, mechanism in hand, bill itemized (OSIV off, ADR-007). Under hostile review, the fought defaults are your strongest exhibits, if each one has a tab.

Story anchors

The ADR binder on the conference table, sixteen tabs, read overnight by a stranger → defensibility: the auditor attacks decisions, and decisions with records (context, -ility, rejected alternatives, exit criteria) defend themselves.
Imane's four-beat 409 answer, "the error you can see over the corruption you can't" → the succession proof: the skeleton transmitted whole, and the architect's silence as the final teaching move.
The two concessions drying in green on the Wall → "the architecture has a mechanism for being wrong": an architect's authority is the trail of priced decisions plus the demonstrated ability to reopen one.

Interview ammo

Kill-shot: The final gate: defend a whole system under hostile questioning. Don't defend the code; defend the decisions, each in four beats, grounded in a named incident, traced to a dated record that names its own revisit conditions. When the questioner finds a decision whose context has really moved, concede on the spot and price the fix. The concession is the senior answer.
Follow-up: An auditor attacks a decision you now believe is wrong. What do you do? Defend the decision as made (its context, its price at the time), then reopen it on the record: name what changed, sketch the remediation's mechanism and cost, attach an owner and a date. Never defend the present with the past's threat model.
Follow-up: How do you retrofit revocation onto stateless JWTs, and what does it really cost? A denylist of token IDs checked in the bearer filter, entries expiring with their token's TTL so the set stays bounded. The bill is one shared-store lookup per request, plus a forced choice between fail-open (revocation silently vanishes when the store blips) and fail-closed (the store joins your availability budget).
Architect follow-up: What distinguishes an over-engineered resilience stack from a priced one? In a priced stack, every component traces to a named incident or an explicitly priced risk: insurance with a claims history and an approved premium. Anything tracing only to a conference talk is ceremony, and anything designed but never drilled is still a hypothesis, whatever the runbook says.
Follow-up: Which production incident of your own would you bring to this room? One with a name and a postmortem, told in the same four beats and tied to the decision it bought. Kenza's model is the April outage: Tomcat threads parked behind one slow vendor with CPUs idle, the whole site answering 503, and ADR-006's timeout policy as what the outage bought.

The Architect's Principles
Nineteen sentences the year wrote in green. Each one is a scene first: recall the scene, and the principle argues itself.

"Works" is not "done". Senior code is judged by how it survives, not whether it runs. Scene: the 47 green-ink comments on a feature that ran flawlessly in the demo (Ch.1).
Every boundary you respect is an option you still own, and the seam, not the conference, decides when to exercise it. Evolvability is the option ledger. Scene: the January seams the November split ran along (Ch.1/14).
Testability is evolvability's leading indicator. A class you can't construct in a unit test is architecture you can't change cheaply. Scene: new ReportDigestService() with nothing to pass (Ch.1).
An architecture you don't enforce is a rumor. Review vigilance decays and fitness functions don't. Scene: the red CI build naming its own law, a fortnight after its author broke it (Ch.2).
No annotation is magic: the advice lives in the proxy, and this. walks around it. Show me the mechanism, or the mechanism will show you. Scene: the half-saved triage states (Ch.3).
A bean nobody can explain is a bean nobody owns. Config is a schema, and absence is a failure class with a test. Scene: eight engineers silent at standup over a vanished health bean (Ch.4).
Every error a user sees is a designed response or a security leak. The error surface is part of the contract. Scene: @sable's 500 with the JDBC URL in it (Ch.5).
Availability is arithmetic before it is architecture. Pool ÷ residence time is the ceiling, and residence belongs to your slowest dependency. Scene: the napkin, 7/s × 30 s > 200 threads (Ch.6).
Performance is a designed property, declared in the query and asserted in CI, never a patch. Scene: the 28-second dashboard's 401 individually flawless statements (Ch.7).
Lean on the framework where the default's -ility bill is one you'd pay anyway; fight it only on the record, mechanism in hand. Scene: OSIV switched off with a tab in the binder, the fought default as strongest exhibit (Ch.7/17).
Choose the error you can see over the corruption you can't. Integrity means picking your consistency model on purpose. Scene: the 409 Imane defended to the auditors (Ch.8/17).
The aggregate is the unit of consistency and of change. Invariants stay inside one transaction, and IDs go across the line. Scene: three chalk boxes that grew into the context map (Ch.9/14).
Fail closed is a structural property, not a vigilance program. Security lives where forgetting is safe. Scene: anyRequest().denyAll() and the route that drifted (Ch.10).
The test suite is the system's second architecture, the one that makes changing the first cheap. It is evolvability's enabler. Scene: forty distrusted minutes becoming trusted ones (Ch.11).
Observability is designed at feature time: what will 3 a.m. ask, and is the answer already recorded? The -ility is operability. Scene: the page that arrived with zero data (Ch.12).
Backpressure is a system property, not a queue setting, and a fallback that lies is an incident you've scheduled for later. Availability is honestly refusing the load you can't survive. Scene: the smoke cloud and the pending badge (Ch.13).
Bet settings, not codebases. Reversibility is the -ility that keeps every other bet survivable, and cost is priced in dollars, risk, and team. Scene: virtual threads as a property flip, reactive as a one-way door (Ch.15).
A defensible architecture is a body of evidence with a working appeals process, written for the next engineer, not the next meeting. Defensibility is the -ility above the others. Scene: sixteen tabs on the due-diligence table, two concessions drying in green, the pen changing desks (Ch.16/17).
Know which door you're in. Two-way doors reward optionality; one-way doors (the public contract, the consistency model) reward decisive commitment, because deferring those means deciding later under worse information. Scene: the version-from-day-one reveal (Ch.5) and the conflict contract (Ch.8).

Fetch in the query (a plan per view), project to DTOs (mapping types forever), or hold the session open via OSIV, which hides N+1s and keeps the request's connection until rendering ends. OSIV is the default ADR-007 turned off on the record.

Why didn't the transaction roll back?

@Version turns the lost update into a visible 409 the user resolves; pessimistic relocates the cost into a row lock held across human think time. Choose by contention shape and hold time.

The unit of consistency and change: invariants inside one transaction, by-ID references across the line, cross-aggregate reads as read models. It is the context map at smaller scale (ADR-009).

Your event arrived twice. Whose bug?
Nobody's: at-least-once is the contract. The outbox writes the event inside the business transaction and a relay publishes it, so the consumer dedupes by event ID; idempotency is the receiver's half of the pattern.


Eureka, evaluated and declined (Ch.14)
Why no service registry on Kubernetes?
A k8s Service is the registry: DNS name, kube-proxy load balancing, readiness-driven eviction. Eureka there is a second discovery system to disagree with the first (ADR-014).


 on the war-room screen (Ch.15)
Virtual threads vs WebFlux, and the catch?
Virtual threads keep thread-per-request semantics and unmount on blocking I/O, except when pinned (synchronized plus blocking, on that JDK); audit with JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, which fires only when a pinned thread parks, and with jdk.JavaMonitorEnter, its 20 ms threshold lowered, for a contended monitor whose holder never parks; quarantine vendor code on a platform pool. You bet a setting, reactive bets the codebase (ADR-015).


Notifications starting in 80 ms after a nine-minute build (Ch.15)
When does native image pay?
Scale-to-zero, CLIs, serverless: startup and memory bought with build time and a closed world (declare your reflection); a hot, JIT-warmed monolith is the opposite end of the curve (ADR-015).


The empty chair at the whiteboard (Ch.16)
"Design duplicate detection." Go.
Clarify load, accuracy, and the cost asymmetry first; then contract → data → transactions → failures → observability → rollout. That yields an async advisory pipeline off the outbox, and only a human merges, because the domain owns truth (ADR-016).


The ADR binder on the due-diligence table (Ch.17)
Defend this architecture.
Defend decisions, not code: four beats each, grounded in named incidents, traced to dated records that name their own revisit conditions. Where the context has moved, concede and price the fix in the room; the concession is the senior answer.
